title: Neural networks and backpropagation
lead: How a stack of linear maps and nonlinearities learns its own features, how reverse-mode differentiation delivers the whole gradient for at most two more forward passes, and why training is mostly a matter of keeping numbers in range: initialisation, optimisers, normalisation, regularisation and numerical stability, each with the check that shows when it has failed.
prerequisites: Module 01: the supervised-learning set-up, losses as negative log-likelihoods (squared error, binary and softmax cross-entropy), gradient descent and mini-batch SGD, the condition number and why features are standardised, train/validation/test splits, ridge regression as weight decay, and early stopping.
Calculus: partial derivatives, the multivariable chain rule as a sum over paths, and the second-order Taylor expansion.
Linear algebra: matrix products and their shapes, the transpose, outer products, and the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix.
Probability: expectation and variance, the variance of a sum of independent variables, and the Bernoulli distribution.
Python with NumPy (array shapes, broadcasting, the `@` operator); no PyTorch is assumed, because it is introduced as it is used, from Lab 1's cross-check onwards.
outcomes: Write the forward pass of an $L$-layer MLP for a batch with every shape stated, and count its parameters, its forward FLOPs (two per weight per example) and the activations it must store.

Derive the four backpropagation equations from the chain rule, including $\boldsymbol{\delta} = \hat{\mathbf{p}} - \mathbf{y}$ for softmax cross-entropy, and implement them in NumPy so that every gradient entry agrees with central finite differences to a relative error below $10^{-6}$.

Explain backpropagation as reverse-mode automatic differentiation on a computational graph, compute a gradient by hand in both forward and reverse mode, and say why reverse mode costs a small multiple of the forward pass for a scalar loss while forward mode needs one pass per input.
Derive Xavier (Glorot) and He initialisation from variance preservation, and predict layer by layer what zero, too-small and too-large initial scales do to activations and gradients.

Implement SGD, heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam with its derived bias correction, and AdamW, give the stability limits of gradient descent and momentum on a quadratic, and explain why decoupled weight decay differs from $L_2$ regularisation under Adam.
Choose a peak learning rate with a range test, configure warmup and cosine decay, and apply global-norm gradient clipping, knowing what each protects against.
Compute batch norm, layer norm and RMSNorm by hand, and state how batch norm behaves differently in training and evaluation mode.
Derive the $1/(1 - p)$ scaling of inverted dropout, and use weight decay, early stopping, augmentation, label smoothing and temperature scaling for what each actually does.

Compute cross-entropy from logits without overflow by log-sum-exp, explain why $\ln(\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}))$ and a softmax placed before the loss fail, and state the ranges of fp32, bf16 and fp16.
Diagnose a failing run from its initial loss, loss curves, gradient norms and activation statistics, using the overfit-one-batch test, gradient checks and a written checklist.
software: PyTorch 2.x; the CPU build is enough, and Google Colab is a free alternative.
scikit-learn, using only `load_digits` and `make_moons`, which ship with the package, so nothing is downloaded.
A current web browser for the two interactive widgets.

sections.title: From fixed features to learned ones
sections.purpose: Show why a network that learns its own features can fit what a linear model on fixed features cannot, state exactly what the universal approximation theorem promises, and show with a counting argument why depth buys more than width.
must_cover: Open from Module 01: a linear model on hand-made features, f(x) = w⊤φ(x), works when someone knows φ. A neural network makes the feature map part of the model and learns it: f(x) = w⊤h(x; θ) with h = φ(W⊤x + b).

Define the MLP in this module's convention, used everywhere afterwards: h⁽⁰⁾ = x; z⁽ˡ⁾ = W⁽ˡ⁾⊤h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾; h⁽ˡ⁾ = φ(z⁽ˡ⁾) for l = 1 … L−1; the last layer has no φ and outputs z⁽ᴸ⁾ (a prediction for regression, logits for classification), which the loss consumes (squared error; softmax cross-entropy). W⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(d_{l−1} × d_l), b⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(d_l); φ is a fixed nonlinear function applied elementwise. Name the parts: input, hidden layer, hidden unit, output layer, width, depth.
Why the nonlinearity is necessary, written out: without φ, z⁽²⁾ = W⁽²⁾⊤(W⁽¹⁾⊤x + b⁽¹⁾) + b⁽²⁾ = (W⁽¹⁾W⁽²⁾)⊤x + (W⁽²⁾⊤b⁽¹⁾ + b⁽²⁾), an affine map; any depth of affine layers collapses to one.

The universal approximation theorem stated precisely: for any continuous f on a compact set K ⊂ ℝ^d and any ε > 0 there is a finite width N and weights such that a one-hidden-layer network g satisfies sup over x in K of |f(x) − g(x)| < ε (Cybenko 1989 for sigmoids; Hornik 1991; Leshno et al. 1993 for any non-polynomial activation, which includes ReLU).

Three things it does not say: how large N must be (constructions grid the input and can need a number of units exponential in d); whether gradient descent from a random start finds such weights; whether a network fitted to finitely many samples generalises. The rest of this module is about the second; Module 01's evaluation discipline is about the third.

The theorem made constructive in one dimension: on [a, b] with knots x₀ < … < x_K, the piecewise-linear interpolant of f is exactly a one-hidden-layer ReLU network g(x) = f(x₀) + Σ_{k=0}^{K−1} c_k ReLU(x − x_k), with c₀ the first segment's slope and c_k the change of slope at knot k. For equal spacing h the error is at most M h²/8 with M = max |f''| (state the bound and derive it from the remainder of linear interpolation in two lines).

Why depth helps (Telgarsky 2016): the tent map t(x) = 2ReLU(x) − 4ReLU(x − ½) on [0, 1] uses two ReLU units. Composing it k times gives a sawtooth with 2^k linear pieces using 2 units per layer: 2k units and 6k + 1 parameters (first layer 4, each further layer 6, output 3). A one-hidden-layer ReLU network with n units on a scalar input is piecewise linear with breakpoints only at x = −b_j/w_j, so it has at most n + 1 pieces; representing t^k therefore needs at least 2^k − 1 units and 3(2^k − 1) + 1 parameters. Composition reuses the same units on every piece; width pays for every piece separately.

Say honestly what the depth argument shows: functions exist that a deep network represents exponentially more cheaply (the number of linear regions can grow exponentially with depth, Montúfar et al. 2014). It does not show that the functions you care about are such functions, nor that gradient descent finds the construction. Depth also brings the vanishing-gradient problem (s3), which s5, s6 and s10 address. The informal case for depth is that real data look compositional (edges, textures, parts in Module 03).

The learned features are visible: each first-layer ReLU unit is a ridge function, zero on one side of the line w⊤x + b = 0 and rising linearly on the other; the output layer adds them, so a one-hidden-layer ReLU classifier's decision boundary is a polygon. The mlp-playground widget shows these unit maps live; point the reader to its three suggested experiments.
worked_examples: Affine collapse with numbers: W⁽¹⁾ = [[1, 2], [0, 1]] (rows index inputs), b⁽¹⁾ = (1, 0), W⁽²⁾ = [[1], [−1]], b⁽²⁾ = 0.5, no activation. Then z⁽¹⁾ = (x₁ + 1, 2x₁ + x₂) and z⁽²⁾ = (x₁ + 1) − (2x₁ + x₂) + 0.5 = −x₁ − x₂ + 1.5; equivalently W⁽¹⁾W⁽²⁾ = [[−1], [−1]] and W⁽²⁾⊤b⁽¹⁾ + b⁽²⁾ = 1.5. One straight line, whatever the depth.

Constructive approximation of f(x) = sin 3x on [−1, 1] (the function of Lab 1): M = 9, h = 2/K, bound 9(2/K)²/8 = 4.5/K². Measured maximum errors: K = 6 gives 0.122 (bound 0.125); K = 16 gives 0.0174; K = 22 gives 0.0093 (bound 0.0093), so 22 ReLU units reach ε = 0.01. For K = 6 the hinge coefficients are c = (−2.304, 2.508, 2.321, 0, −2.321, −2.508): the fourth is exactly zero because the slopes either side of x = 0 are equal (2.524), so 5 units suffice. Contrast with Lab 1, where gradient descent on 64 units reaches a training mean squared error of 2.8×10⁻⁴ (RMS error 0.017) in 3,000 steps, with no guarantee that it would.

Sawtooth counting, checked numerically on a fine grid: t^k has 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 pieces for k = 1 … 6. For k = 10 the deep construction has 20 units and 61 parameters; a one-hidden-layer network needs at least 1,023 units and 3,070 parameters. For k = 20: 121 parameters against at least 3,145,726.

The playground on the circles data (200 training points; numbers from a NumPy simulation of the widget's specification, so the widget itself will differ slightly): no hidden layer gives 53.5% training accuracy at loss 0.692 = ln 2, i.e. chance; three hidden layers with the identity activation give exactly the same 53.5%; one hidden layer of 2 ReLU units reaches 84.5% (two half-planes cannot enclose a disc); 3 units reach 100% after about 245 Adam steps (a triangle); 8 units after about 58. On the two-arm spiral, 2 hidden layers of 16 units (337 parameters) fit the training set in about 740 steps, 1 layer of 64 units (257 parameters) in about 2,430, 1 layer of 128 (513 parameters) in about 1,830, and 1 layer of 16 reaches only 74% in 3,000 steps: an illustration of depth, not a proof.

checks: A network with three hidden layers but no activation functions is trained on the circles data. What boundaries can it represent? -> Only straight lines: a composition of affine maps is affine, so it is logistic regression with extra parameters.
A one-hidden-layer ReLU network with 5 hidden units takes a scalar input. At most how many linear pieces can its output have? -> 6: each unit adds at most one breakpoint, at x = −b/w.

Does the universal approximation theorem guarantee that gradient descent on a wide enough network will fit a given continuous function? -> No. It guarantees that suitable weights exist; it says nothing about finding them or about generalising from finite data.

sections.title: The forward pass, with shapes
sections.purpose: Make the forward computation for a batch concrete — shapes, parameter counts, FLOPs and stored activations — because most bugs are shape bugs and every cost estimate later in the series starts here.
must_cover: The batch convention: B inputs stacked as rows, H⁽⁰⁾ = X ∈ ℝ^(B × d₀); Z⁽ˡ⁾ = H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾W⁽ˡ⁾ + 1b⁽ˡ⁾⊤ ∈ ℝ^(B × d_l); H⁽ˡ⁾ = φ(Z⁽ˡ⁾). The bias is broadcast over rows (in NumPy, adding shape (d_l,) to (B, d_l)). One example is one row; the column form z = W⊤h + b of s1 is the same computation transposed.
The output Z⁽ᴸ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(B × K) holds logits for K classes; the softmax happens inside the loss (s12), never as a layer in front of it.
Parameter count Σ_l (d_{l−1}d_l + d_l).

FLOPs: a (B × m)(m × n) product costs 2Bmn FLOPs (Bmn multiplies and about as many adds). Summed over layers the forward pass costs about 2B × (number of weights): each weight is touched once by a multiply and once by an add per example. Bias adds and activations cost O(B·d_l) per layer, negligible for wide layers. This is where the rule of thumb '2N FLOPs per token per forward pass' for large models comes from. Module 06 owns the series' FLOP convention; state it here once, in two sentences, with a link to Module 06, Section 11: in a FLOP count N means the weights used in matrix products (an embedding lookup costs no FLOPs), attention adds a term that grows with the context, and a training step is counted as three forward passes (s3 shows why backward costs at most twice forward); memory counts every parameter. Do not give the attention formula, which only Module 06 states.

Memory: the backward pass (s3) needs each layer's input H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ and its Z⁽ˡ⁾ (or enough to evaluate φ'), so a training forward pass stores O(B·Σ d_l) numbers. Parameters are stored once; activations once per example in the batch — which is why activation memory grows with batch × depth. State the byte units once, here: kB, MB and GB are decimal (10³, 10⁶, 10⁹ bytes), KiB, MiB and GiB binary (2¹⁰, 2²⁰, 2³⁰ bytes); the one binary quantity that recurs, the deep MLP's 100 MiB tape (s2, s4), is also given in decimal units.

PyTorch's nn.Linear(d_in, d_out) stores its weight as (d_out, d_in) and computes x W⊤ + b. The mathematics is identical; only the stored layout differs, which matters when copying weights between NumPy and PyTorch (Lab 1 does exactly this).

Shape discipline: write the shape beside every array in comments or assertions. The commonest silent shape bug in regression: a prediction of shape (B, 1) minus a target of shape (B,) broadcasts to (B, B). NumPy computes it silently; PyTorch's F.mse_loss emits 'Using a target size … that is different to the input size … This will likely lead to incorrect results due to broadcasting', and the model learns to predict the mean, with the loss stuck at the variance of the targets.
worked_examples: The running tiny network, reused in s3 and s4: x = (2, 1); W⁽¹⁾ = [[0.5, −1.0], [0.25, 0.5]] (rows index inputs, columns index hidden units); b⁽¹⁾ = (0.1, 0); ReLU; W⁽²⁾ = [[0.8], [−0.6]]; b⁽²⁾ = 0.2; target t = 1; loss (ŷ − t)². Forward: z⁽¹⁾ = W⁽¹⁾⊤x + b⁽¹⁾ = (0.5·2 + 0.25·1 + 0.1, −1·2 + 0.5·1 + 0) = (1.35, −1.5); h⁽¹⁾ = (1.35, 0); ŷ = 0.8·1.35 − 0.6·0 + 0.2 = 1.28; loss 0.28² = 0.0784. Nine parameters; 12 FLOPs in the two products (8 in layer 1, 4 in layer 2) plus the bias adds.

The digits network of Labs 3–5, 64 → 128 → 128 → 10: parameters 64·128 + 128 + 128·128 + 128 + 128·10 + 10 = 8,320 + 16,512 + 1,290 = 26,122 (104,488 bytes in fp32), of which 25,856 are weights. Forward FLOPs 2 × 25,856 = 51,712 per example; for a batch of 64, 1,048,576 + 2,097,152 + 163,840 = 3,309,568 ≈ 3.3 MFLOPs. Stored activations for B = 64 (input, Z and H of both hidden layers, logits): (64 + 2·128 + 2·128 + 10) × 64 × 4 bytes = 150,016 bytes, more than the parameters.

Scale: an MLP of 50 layers of width 1,024 has 52.5 million parameters (210 MB in fp32); storing Z and H for a batch of 256 takes 2 × 50 × 256 × 1,024 × 4 = 104,857,600 bytes = 100 MiB (105 MB), and at batch 4,096 about 1.6 GiB (1.7 GB) — activations, not parameters, set training memory once batches are large. A model with 7×10⁹ parameters needs roughly 2 × 7×10⁹ = 1.4×10¹⁰ FLOPs per token for a forward pass: an estimate that treats every parameter as a matrix weight and ignores attention, which Module 06, Section 11 refines.

The broadcasting trap measured (PyTorch, sin 3x on 256 points, targets of shape (256,), predictions (256, 1), Adam for 2,000 steps): the warning fires on every step, the predictions collapse to a constant (standard deviation 0.0006), and the 'loss' settles at 0.5174, exactly the variance of the targets.

checks: X has shape (32, 64) and W⁽¹⁾ has shape (64, 128). What is the shape of Z⁽¹⁾ and the cost of the product? -> (32, 128); 2·32·64·128 = 524,288 FLOPs.

A regression model outputs shape (B, 1) and the targets have shape (B,). What does NumPy compute for (pred − t)², and what does a model trained on it learn? -> A (B, B) matrix of all pairwise differences; its mean is minimised by predicting the mean target everywhere, so the loss stalls at the variance of the targets.

sections.title: Backpropagation: the four equations
sections.purpose: Derive backpropagation from the chain rule, so that every line of a backward pass can be written, checked and costed by hand.
must_cover: A matrix-calculus refresher, where it is first needed: the gradient of a scalar with respect to a vector or matrix has the shape of that vector or matrix; the Jacobian of y = f(x), y ∈ ℝ^m, x ∈ ℝ^n, is J ∈ ℝ^(m × n) with J_ij = ∂y_i/∂x_j; the chain rule composes Jacobians, J_{g∘f} = J_g J_f; for a scalar loss, ∇_x𝓛 = J_f⊤∇_y𝓛. Three facts used everywhere: (i) z = W⊤h + b gives ∂z/∂h = W⊤, so ∇_h𝓛 = W∇_z𝓛; (ii) ∂𝓛/∂W_ij = h_i ∂𝓛/∂z_j, so ∇_W𝓛 = h(∇_z𝓛)⊤, an outer product; (iii) an elementwise h = φ(z) has the diagonal Jacobian diag(φ'(z)), so ∇_z𝓛 = ∇_h𝓛 ⊙ φ'(z). Use shapes to decide where the transposes go.
Define the error signal δ⁽ˡ⁾ = ∂𝓛/∂z⁽ˡ⁾ for one example (a column vector of length d_l).

Equation 1, at the output. Module 01 derived ∂ℓ/∂z = p̂ − y for softmax cross-entropy case by case; re-derive it here in two lines as the first use of the Jacobian refresher: 𝓛 = −Σ_k y_k log p̂_k with p̂ = softmax(z) has the softmax Jacobian ∂p̂/∂z = diag(p̂) − p̂p̂⊤ (entries p̂_k(𝟙[k = j] − p̂_j)), so ∂𝓛/∂z_j = −Σ_k y_k(𝟙[k = j] − p̂_j) = p̂_j − y_j, i.e. δ⁽ᴸ⁾ = p̂ − y — the same p̂ − y as logistic regression. Its entries sum to zero. For squared error with a linear output, δ⁽ᴸ⁾ = 2(ŷ − y). With the loss averaged over a batch, each example's δ carries a factor 1/B.

Equation 2, between layers: z⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ = W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾⊤φ(z⁽ˡ⁾) + b⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾, so δ⁽ˡ⁾_i = Σ_j δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾_j W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾_ij φ'(z⁽ˡ⁾_i), i.e. δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ φ'(z⁽ˡ⁾): the error is pushed back through the weights and gated by the activation's derivative.
Equations 3 and 4, the parameter gradients: ∂𝓛/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾δ⁽ˡ⁾⊤ (shape d_{l−1} × d_l, the shape of W⁽ˡ⁾) and ∂𝓛/∂b⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾. 'Those four equations are the whole algorithm.'

The batch form: with Δ⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(B × d_l) stacking the δ⊤ of the batch, Δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (Δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾⊤) ⊙ φ'(Z⁽ˡ⁾); ∂𝓛/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾⊤Δ⁽ˡ⁾ (the sum over the batch of outer products); ∂𝓛/∂b⁽ˡ⁾ = the column sums of Δ⁽ˡ⁾. Map each line to Lab 1's backward function: dY = 2*(Y − T)/B; g['W2'] = H1.T @ dY; dH1 = dY @ W2.T; dZ1 = dH1 * (Z1 > 0); g['W1'] = X.T @ dZ1.
The algorithm as a box: a forward pass that stores Z⁽ˡ⁾ and H⁽ˡ⁾, then one backward sweep for l = L … 1.

Cost: each layer's backward does two products the size of its forward product (ΔW⊤ for the error passed down, H⊤Δ for the weight gradient), so backward ≤ 2 × forward and a training step costs at most about 3 forward passes. The first layer's input gradient is never needed, so the ratio is below 2 when the first layer dominates. Keep only this argument: Module 06 owns the training-FLOP count for transformers, so one sentence links Module 06, Section 11 for it, under the convention stated in s2; no 6N formula is written here.

Consequence 1 (source): δ⁽ˡ⁾ is a product of L − l Jacobians W⁽ᵏ⁾diag(φ'(z⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾)); if their norms are below 1 the gradient vanishes with depth, above 1 it explodes. Sigmoid networks of ten layers did not train in the 1990s for this reason (φ' ≤ 1/4); ReLU, careful initialisation, normalisation and residual connections are the fixes, in that historical order (s5, s6, s10).

Consequence 2 (source): the gradient of a weight matrix is the outer product of what came in and the error that went out, so every layer's input must be kept from the forward pass: training memory scales with depth × batch, and gradient checkpointing (recompute instead of store, s4) exists for this reason.
worked_examples: The backward pass of the s2 network by hand: δ⁽²⁾ = 2(1.28 − 1) = 0.56; ∂𝓛/∂W⁽²⁾ = h⁽¹⁾δ⁽²⁾ = (1.35·0.56, 0·0.56) = (0.756, 0); ∂𝓛/∂b⁽²⁾ = 0.56; δ⁽¹⁾ = (W⁽²⁾δ⁽²⁾) ⊙ φ'(z⁽¹⁾) = (0.8·0.56, −0.6·0.56) ⊙ (1, 0) = (0.448, 0); ∂𝓛/∂W⁽¹⁾ = xδ⁽¹⁾⊤ = [[0.896, 0], [0.448, 0]]; ∂𝓛/∂b⁽¹⁾ = (0.448, 0). The inactive second unit (z = −1.5) passes no gradient, so its incoming weights learn nothing from this example. Check one entry by central differences with ε = 10⁻³: 𝓛 at W⁽¹⁾₁₁ ± ε is 0.07929856 and 0.07750656, and (0.07929856 − 0.07750656)/0.002 = 0.896000.

sections.title: Automatic differentiation: graphs, reverse mode and forward mode
sections.purpose: Show that backpropagation is one instance of reverse-mode automatic differentiation on a computational graph, why reverse mode is the right mode for a scalar loss, and what PyTorch is doing when you call loss.backward().
must_cover: A computational graph: nodes are primitive operations (add, multiply, matrix product, exp, log, sin, tanh, ReLU); edges carry intermediate values v_i in an evaluation (topological) order. Each primitive knows its local partial derivatives.

Forward mode: carry a tangent v̇_i alongside each value, v̇_i = Σ over parents j of (∂v_i/∂v_j)·v̇_j. Seeding the inputs with a direction u gives, in one pass, the Jacobian-vector product J u (a directional derivative). Dual numbers a + bε with ε² = 0 implement it: f(a + bε) = f(a) + f'(a)b ε.

Reverse mode: after the forward pass, carry adjoints v̄_i = ∂𝓛/∂v_i backwards, v̄_j += v̄_i·∂v_i/∂v_j for every child i of j. The '+=' is the multivariable chain rule: a variable used in several places receives the sum of the contributions of every path. One pass gives a vector-Jacobian product u⊤J; for a scalar loss (u = 1) that is the whole gradient.

The cost argument: for f: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ the full Jacobian costs n forward-mode passes (a column each) or m reverse-mode passes (a row each), each a small constant multiple of evaluating f (the 'cheap gradient principle'; Griewank and Walther 2008). Training has m = 1 and n from 10⁴ to 10¹¹, so reverse mode wins by a factor of order n. Forward mode wins when n ≪ m: the sensitivity of a simulated trajectory (m = 1,000 outputs) to 3 design parameters, or Hessian-vector products (forward over reverse). Physics-informed networks (Module 05) differentiate the network with respect to its few inputs, a natural forward-mode use.

The price of reverse mode is memory: the backward sweep needs the forward values, so they are stored (the 'tape'). Gradient checkpointing stores only some layers' activations and recomputes the rest during the backward pass; storing every √L-th layer cuts activation memory from O(L) to O(√L) for about one extra forward pass (Chen et al. 2016).

Layers as VJP rules: for z = W⊤h + b, given z̄: h̄ = Wz̄, W̄ = hz̄⊤, b̄ = z̄ (exactly s3's equations); for h = φ(z): z̄ = h̄ ⊙ φ'(z); for softmax cross-entropy: z̄ = p̂ − y. Frameworks never form a Jacobian: for a 4,096 → 4,096 layer and a batch of 512, the Jacobian of all outputs with respect to all inputs would have (512 · 4,096)² ≈ 4.4×10¹² entries, while the VJP is one matrix product.

How PyTorch does it: each operation on tensors that require gradients records a node (visible as tensor.grad_fn) holding what its backward needs; loss.backward() walks the graph in reverse topological order and accumulates into each leaf's .grad with '+='; the graph is rebuilt on every forward pass (define-by-run) and freed after backward. torch.no_grad() stops recording (evaluation, and the optimiser's own updates); .detach() cuts a tensor out of the graph, which silently stops gradients if done by mistake. Because .grad accumulates across backward calls, each optimiser step must be preceded by optimizer.zero_grad(): the same '+=' that makes the chain rule work makes a forgotten zero_grad sum all past gradients (Lab 5, script B).

The bridge to Lab 2: a scalar engine of about 100 lines implements exactly this, and shows why frameworks work on tensors rather than scalars (66,440 scalar nodes per step for a 337-parameter network on 100 examples, against about ten tensor operations).
worked_examples: Both modes by hand on f(x₁, x₂) = ln x₁ + x₁x₂ − sin x₂ at (2, 5), the running example of Baydin et al. (2018). Forward values: v₁ = ln 2 = 0.6931; v₂ = 2·5 = 10; v₃ = sin 5 = −0.9589; v₄ = v₁ + v₂ = 10.6931; f = v₄ − v₃ = 11.6521. Forward mode with tangent (1, 0): v̇₁ = 1/2 = 0.5; v̇₂ = 1·5 + 2·0 = 5; v̇₃ = cos 5 · 0 = 0; ḟ = 5.5 = ∂f/∂x₁; a second pass with tangent (0, 1) gives ∂f/∂x₂ = 0 + 2 − cos 5 = 1.7163. Reverse mode, one pass: f̄ = 1; v̄₄ = 1; v̄₃ = −1; v̄₁ = 1; v̄₂ = 1; x̄₂ = v̄₂·x₁ + v̄₃·cos 5 = 2 − 0.2837 = 1.7163; x̄₁ = v̄₁/x₁ + v̄₂·x₂ = 0.5 + 5 = 5.5 — x₁ is used twice and its adjoint is the sum of the two paths.

Pass counts: the digits network has 26,122 parameters, so a forward-mode gradient needs 26,122 passes against one reverse pass costing about 1.7 forward passes more. A 7×10⁹-parameter model would need 7×10⁹ forward-mode passes.

Checkpointing in numbers: for the 50-layer, width-1,024 MLP of s2 at batch 256, each layer's Z and H take 2 MiB and the full tape 100 MiB (105 MB). Checkpointing every 7th layer (√50 ≈ 7) holds about 50/7 + 7 ≈ 14 layers' worth at a time, roughly 28 MiB (29 MB), for one extra forward pass.

What does optimizer.zero_grad() protect against? -> PyTorch adds each backward pass's gradients into .grad; without zeroing, every step uses the sum of all previous gradients.

sections.title: Activation functions
sections.purpose: Choose activations knowing their derivatives, because the derivative is what backpropagation multiplies by at every layer.
must_cover: The source's table, extended, with formula, derivative, range, zero-centred or not, where it saturates, and typical use: sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)), σ' = σ(1 − σ) ≤ 1/4, range (0, 1), not zero-centred, saturates on both sides, used for binary output probabilities and gates (Module 04); tanh, 1 − tanh², (−1, 1), zero-centred, saturates on both sides; ReLU max(0, z), 𝟙[z > 0], [0, ∞), not zero-centred, exactly zero on the left; leaky ReLU max(az, z) with a = 0.01, derivative a or 1; GELU zΦ(z) with Φ the standard normal CDF, derivative Φ(z) + zφ_N(z) with φ_N the standard normal density, smooth, the transformer default (BERT, GPT-2); SiLU/Swish zσ(z), derivative σ(z)(1 + z(1 − σ(z))), smooth, used in the gated feed-forward blocks (SwiGLU) of most open large language models as of 2026 (Module 06).
Derive σ' = σ(1 − σ), and show tanh z = 2σ(2z) − 1: tanh is a rescaled sigmoid whose derivative at 0 is 1 instead of 1/4.
Saturation: where φ' ≈ 0 a unit passes almost no gradient (σ'(5) = 0.0066, tanh'(3) = 0.0099). A saturated unit is not dead for ever, but it learns at a rate set by that tiny derivative.

Why ReLU won (source): a derivative of exactly 1 on the active side passes errors through many layers undiminished, where sigmoids multiply them by at most 1/4 per layer; it is also cheap to compute. GELU and SiLU keep the near-linear positive side and add smoothness.

GELU and SiLU are not monotonic: GELU has its minimum −0.170 at z = −0.752 and SiLU −0.278 at z = −1.278, with slightly negative derivatives below those points. GELU's tanh approximation 0.5z(1 + tanh(√(2/π)(z + 0.044715z³))) differs from the exact form by at most 4.7×10⁻⁴; PyTorch's nn.GELU() uses the exact erf form by default and nn.GELU(approximate='tanh') the approximation.

Zero-centring: a sigmoid layer's outputs are all positive, so for one example every gradient ∂𝓛/∂W_ij = h_iδ_j into unit j has the sign of δ_j; the incoming weight vector can only move in directions whose components share a sign, which zig-zags. tanh, and zero-mean inputs (s6, s10), avoid it.

Dead ReLU units: if a unit's pre-activation is negative for every training example, its derivative is zero everywhere, its incoming weights and bias receive zero gradient, and plain gradient descent can never revive it (exercise e5). Causes: a large update (too high a learning rate) that pushes the bias far negative; a poor initialisation. Remedies: a lower learning rate, He initialisation (s6), leaky ReLU or GELU. Measure the dead fraction (units with output 0 for the whole batch), as Labs 4 and 5 do.
The output layer is different: its 'activation' is fixed by the loss (identity for squared error; logits into a softmax or sigmoid inside a cross-entropy, s12) and is never chosen for gradient flow.
worked_examples: Attenuation through ten layers from the activation derivatives alone: sigmoid at its best point 0.25¹⁰ = 9.5×10⁻⁷; tanh at z = 0, 1; ReLU on its active side, 1.
Second moment against variance through a ReLU: for z ~ 𝒩(0, 1), E[ReLU(z)²] = 0.5 but Var(ReLU(z)) = 0.5 − 1/(2π) = 0.341. s6 needs the second moment.

Dead units caused by the learning rate (the playground's circles problem, NumPy simulation of the widget's specification): Adam at η = 1 leaves 4 of 8 hidden ReLU units dead; plain gradient descent at η = 10 kills all 8, and the loss sticks at 1.04 with 50% accuracy.

A ReLU unit has bias −10 and small incoming weights, and the inputs are standardised. What happens to it in training? -> Its pre-activation is negative for essentially every input, its gradient is zero, and it stays dead.

sections.title: Initialisation
sections.purpose: Derive the initial weight scale from variance preservation, and show what zero, too-small and too-large scales do to a deep network.
must_cover: Symmetry: with all weights equal (zero or any constant), every unit in a layer computes the same function and receives the same gradient, so the units stay identical for ever; with zero weights and ReLU even the gradient into the first layer is zero. Random weights break the symmetry; biases can start at zero. Rumelhart et al. (1986) already started from small random weights for this reason.

The forward derivation: z_j = Σ_{i=1}^{n} w_ij h_i with the w_ij independent, zero mean, variance σ_w², and independent of h. Then E[z_j] = 0 and Var(z_j) = n σ_w² E[h_i²], because E[(wh)²] = E[w²]E[h²]: the second moment, not Var(h). Correct the source's 'n σ_w² σ_h²', which is right only for zero-mean h.

For tanh near the origin h ≈ z, so E[h²] ≈ Var(z_previous) and preservation needs σ_w² = 1/n_in (LeCun). For ReLU, E[h²] = Var(z_previous)/2 by the symmetry of z, so σ_w² = 2/n_in (He et al. 2015). The source's 'a ReLU halves the variance' should read 'halves the second moment': Var(ReLU(z)) is 0.341 Var(z).

The backward derivation: δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ φ' gives Var(δ⁽ˡ⁾) = n_out σ_w² E[φ'²] Var(δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾), so preservation needs σ_w² = 1/n_out for tanh and 2/n_out for ReLU (E[φ'²] = 1/2). Glorot and Bengio's compromise is σ_w² = 2/(n_in + n_out); in uniform form U(−a, a) with a = √(6/(n_in + n_out)), since Var(U(−a, a)) = a²/3. He et al. show that preserving either direction keeps the other bounded across depth, so fan-in mode is the usual choice for ReLU.

Too large: tanh units saturate (φ' ≈ 0, gradients vanish); ReLU activations grow geometrically and overflow. Too small: signals shrink geometrically, outputs equal the biases, and early-layer gradients are tiny because δ shrinks backwards too — training starts on a plateau (Lab 1's 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴) runs).

Framework defaults are not He: PyTorch's nn.Linear draws weights and biases from U(−1/√n_in, 1/√n_in), a weight variance of 1/(3n_in). Through a stack of ReLU layers this shrinks the second moment 6× per layer until the bias variance sets a floor. For deep ReLU stacks without normalisation, call nn.init.kaiming_normal_ explicitly; shallow networks and networks with normalisation layers tolerate the default (Labs 3–5 use it at depth 3).

Residual connections (source): h⁽ˡ⁾ = h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + f(h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾) has the Jacobian I + ∂f/∂h, so the backward product always contains an identity path and the gradient cannot vanish along it. The forward variance now adds, Var(h⁽ˡ⁾) ≈ Var(h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾) + Var(f), so deep residual networks scale down or zero-initialise the last layer of each branch so that every block starts near the identity. Module 03 introduces them with ResNet and Module 06 shows them in every transformer block.
The output layer: a small output scale makes the initial predictions near-uniform and the initial loss near ln K, which is the first check of s14.
worked_examples: Predicted against measured scale through 10 layers of width 256 (x ~ 𝒩(0, I), 1,000 samples, fixed seed; the standard deviation of z at layers 1, 2, 5 and 10). ReLU with He (2/n): predicted √2 = 1.414 at every layer; measured 1.42, 1.39, 1.46, 1.43. ReLU with 1/n: predicted 2^(−(l−1)/2), i.e. 1, 0.707, 0.25, 0.044; measured 1.01, 0.694, 0.258, 0.0447. ReLU with 𝒩(0, 0.01²): predicted 0.16, then ×0.113 per layer; measured 0.161, 0.0178, 2.7×10⁻⁵, 4.9×10⁻¹⁰. ReLU with PyTorch's default (weights and biases U(±1/16)): measured 0.579, 0.246, 0.0435, 0.0402, settling at the predicted bias floor 0.0395. tanh with 𝒩(0, 1): 16.1, 15.6, 15.5, 15.6, with 87% of the layer-10 outputs beyond |h| = 0.99 (saturated). tanh with 1/n: 1.01, 0.626, 0.356, 0.249, a slow decay because tanh contracts.
Single-layer numbers: fan-in 512 ReLU, He standard deviation √(2/512) = 0.0625; a 784 → 256 layer, Glorot uniform bound √(6/1,040) = 0.0760 and He standard deviation √(2/784) = 0.0505.

The bias floor derived: with weight variance 1/(3n), each ReLU layer multiplies the second moment by n·(1/(3n))·½ = 1/6, and the bias adds Var(b) = 1/(3n); the fixed point of v = v/6 + 1/(3n) is v = 0.4/n, a standard deviation of √(0.4/256) = 0.0395 for n = 256.

sections.title: Gradient descent and momentum
sections.purpose: Explain with the quadratic model why plain gradient descent is slow on ill-conditioned losses, how heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum help, and what limits the learning rate.
must_cover: Recall Module 01 and extend it: on 𝓛 = ½θ⊤Aθ with eigenvalues λ₁ ≤ … ≤ λ_d, gradient descent acts on each eigen-coordinate separately, θ_i ← (1 − ηλ_i)θ_i. It is stable iff η < 2/λ_max; the slowest mode contracts by |1 − ηλ_min| per step; the best fixed η = 2/(λ_max + λ_min) gives the rate (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) with κ = λ_max/λ_min, about κ/2 steps per factor e.

Near a minimum a network's loss is approximately quadratic with the Hessian H in place of A (second-order Taylor expansion), so the same limit η < 2/λ_max(H) applies locally. In full-batch training λ_max(H) tends to rise until it reaches about 2/η and then hovers there (the 'edge of stability', Cohen et al. 2021): the learning rate shapes the curvature the network ends up in.

Stochastic gradients: a mini-batch gradient is the full gradient plus noise whose covariance falls as 1/B (Module 01). The noise makes the loss non-monotone and sets a noise floor proportional to η, which s9 derives and schedules remove.

Heavy-ball momentum (Polyak 1964; the form of Rumelhart et al. 1986 and of PyTorch's SGD): v ← μv + g, θ ← θ − ηv, μ ≈ 0.9. Unrolled, v_t = Σ_k μ^k g_{t−k}, an exponentially weighted sum; for a constant gradient the step tends to ηg/(1 − μ), ten times larger for μ = 0.9 (the effective learning rate η/(1 − μ)). Equivalent form: θ_{t+1} = θ_t − ηg_t + μ(θ_t − θ_{t−1}).

The low-pass-filter view: v is the output of the filter v_t = μv_{t−1} + g_t, whose transfer function is H(ω) = 1/(1 − μe^(−iω)). |H(0)| = 1/(1 − μ) = 10 amplifies the consistent component; |H(π)| = 1/(1 + μ) = 0.53 attenuates a component that flips sign every step. Across a ravine the gradient flips sign and is damped; along it the gradient is consistent and accumulates: a ratio of (1 + μ)/(1 − μ) = 19.

On the quadratic: heavy ball is stable iff 0 < ηλ < 2(1 + μ) for every eigenvalue (from the characteristic equation r² − (1 + μ − ηλ)r + μ = 0); with complex roots the contraction per step is √μ; the optimal parameters η = 4/(√λ_max + √λ_min)² and μ = ((√κ − 1)/(√κ + 1))² give the rate (√κ − 1)/(√κ + 1), about √κ/2 steps per factor e instead of κ/2.

Nesterov momentum: evaluate the gradient at the look-ahead point, v ← μv + ∇𝓛(θ − ημv), θ ← θ − ηv. PyTorch's SGD(nesterov=True) uses an equivalent rewrite that evaluates the gradient at the stored parameters: v ← μv + g, θ ← θ − η(g + μv). It corrects the velocity before overshooting and is faster at moderate η, but its stability limit on the quadratic is smaller: ηλ_max < 2(1 + μ)/(1 + 2μ), which is 1.36 for μ = 0.9, against 2 for GD and 3.8 for heavy ball.

PyTorch conventions: SGD's momentum buffer has no (1 − μ) factor (dampening = 0), unlike Adam's first moment (s8); switching between the two conventions changes the effective learning rate by 1/(1 − μ).

Practice: SGD with momentum 0.9 and a schedule remains strong for convolutional networks (Module 03); the adaptive methods of s8 are the default for transformers. Point the reader to the optimiser-paths widget.
worked_examples: The quadratic 𝓛 = ½(θ₁² + 100θ₂²) (κ = 100), from θ = (1, 1), counting steps until ‖θ‖ < 10⁻³‖θ₀‖ (simulated): GD at the best fixed η = 2/101 = 0.0198 has rate 99/101 = 0.980 and needs 346 steps (345 predicted); GD at η = 0.0201, just above 2/λ_max, diverges. Heavy ball with μ = 0.9 at the same η contracts by √0.9 = 0.949 per step and needs 125 steps. sections.title: Adaptive methods: AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW
sections.purpose: Derive the adaptive optimisers as per-parameter step-size normalisation, including Adam's bias correction, and show exactly why AdamW's decoupled weight decay is not L2 regularisation under Adam.
must_cover: Motivation: gradient scales differ by orders of magnitude across parameters (at step 1 in Lab 3's digits network, from 1.1×10⁻⁸ to 4.4×10⁻²), so a single η is too large for some and too small for others. A diagonal preconditioner D rescales each coordinate: θ ← θ − ηD⁻¹g.

AdaGrad (Duchi et al. 2011): G ← G + g² (elementwise), θ ← θ − ηg/(√G + ε). Rarely updated parameters keep large steps, which suits sparse features; but G only grows, so the effective step decays like 1/√t and long non-convex training stalls.
RMSProp (Tieleman and Hinton 2012, from a lecture slide rather than a paper): replace the sum by an exponential moving average, v ← ρv + (1 − ρ)g², θ ← θ − ηg/(√v + ε), with ρ = 0.9 or 0.99.

Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015): m ← β₁m + (1 − β₁)g; v ← β₂v + (1 − β₂)g²; m̂ = m/(1 − β₁^t); v̂ = v/(1 − β₂^t); θ ← θ − ηm̂/(√v̂ + ε); with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999 (0.95 is common for large language models, where v must follow changes of gradient scale faster) and ε = 10⁻⁸.

Derive the bias correction: with m₀ = 0, m_t = (1 − β₁)Σ_{s=1}^{t} β₁^{t−s}g_s, so for gradients with a constant mean E[m_t] = (1 − β₁^t)E[g]; dividing by 1 − β₁^t removes the bias, and likewise for v. Without correction the step is multiplied by (1 − β₁^t)/√(1 − β₂^t): for β₂ = 0.999 this is 3.16 at t = 1, peaks at 6.57 at t = 12, and is still 1.26 at t = 1,000; for β₂ = 0.95 it is 0.45 at t = 1 and never exceeds 1.10. Which way the error goes depends on β₂ against β₁.

What Adam's step is: |Δθ_i| ≈ η|m̂_i|/√v̂_i, about η when gradients are consistent and less when they are noisy; at t = 1 it is exactly ηg/(|g| + ε) ≈ η·sign(g), so every parameter with a non-negligible gradient moves by η. The update is invariant to rescaling the loss (g → cg leaves m̂/√v̂ unchanged), which is why Adam forgives unscaled losses; it is not invariant to rescaling the parameters, which is why unscaled inputs still hurt (e15).

Adam is per-coordinate: it equalises scales along the parameter axes but cannot undo curvature in rotated directions. The optimiser-paths widget makes this visible: on a ravine aligned with the axes Adam needs 126 steps, rotated by 45° it needs 214, while GD and heavy ball are unaffected by the rotation.

Memory: two extra numbers per parameter. With fp32 weights and gradients that is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes per parameter; with bf16 weights and gradients plus an fp32 master copy, 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes as well (Module 08 does the full accounting). The digits network's 26,122 parameters need 418 kB; 7×10⁹ parameters need 112 GB before any activations.

Weight decay and L2 under SGD: adding (λ/2)‖θ‖² to the loss adds λθ to the gradient, θ ← θ − η(g + λθ) = (1 − ηλ)θ − ηg, which is the same as shrinking the weights by the factor (1 − ηλ) every step. PyTorch's weight_decay = λ corresponds to the penalty (λ/2)‖θ‖²; Module 01 wrote the penalty as λ‖θ‖², which doubles the coefficient.

Under Adam they differ (Loshchilov and Hutter 2019): with L2, g + λθ goes into m and v, and the decay term is divided by √v̂, so parameter i shrinks by about ηλ/√v̂_i per step: parameters with a large gradient history are regularised less, those with small gradients more. AdamW applies the decay outside the normalisation, θ ← θ − η(m̂/(√v̂ + ε) + λθ), shrinking every parameter by the same factor per step (and following the learning-rate schedule). No L2 coefficient reproduces it unless v̂ is the same for every parameter. In PyTorch, torch.optim.AdamW is the decoupled form (default weight_decay 0.01); torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=λ) is the coupled L2 form (default 0); recent versions also accept Adam(..., decoupled_weight_decay=True), which is AdamW.
What to decay: usually the weight matrices, not biases or normalisation gains, which set offsets and scales that decay would only distort; implement it with two parameter groups.
Adam's original convergence proof was later shown to be flawed (Reddi et al. 2018); the method works in practice, and that is the evidence for it.
worked_examples: AdamW against Adam with L2 at η = 10⁻³, λ = 10⁻⁴, for two weights both equal to 1 with gradient RMS 10 and 0.1: Adam + L2 shrinks them by ηλ/√v̂ = 10⁻⁸ and 10⁻⁶ per step, a factor of 100 apart; AdamW shrinks both by ηλ = 10⁻⁷.
Scale invariance: multiply the loss by 1,000. SGD's step becomes 1,000 times larger and diverges at any η that was stable before; Adam's step is unchanged (ε aside).

Adam's first step on the digits network (Lab 3): of 26,122 parameters, 786 have exactly zero gradient (the weights from the four always-zero pixels and from units inactive on that batch); of the rest, 99.9% move by between 0.99η and η although their gradients range from 1.1×10⁻⁸ to 4.4×10⁻².

figures.description: The uncorrected-to-corrected step ratio (1 − β₁^t)/√(1 − β₂^t) against t on a log x-axis from 1 to 10⁴, with β₁ = 0.9: for β₂ = 0.999 rising from 3.16 to a peak of 6.57 at t = 12 and falling to 1; for β₂ = 0.95 rising from 0.45 to a peak of 1.10 at t = 20. A horizontal line at 1.

Log–log plot of the per-step relative shrinkage of a weight against its gradient RMS (10⁻³ to 10²) at η = 10⁻³, λ = 10⁻⁴: AdamW a horizontal line at 10⁻⁷; Adam with L2 a line of slope −1 through 10⁻⁸ at RMS 10 and 10⁻⁶ at RMS 0.1.

checks: Without bias correction and with β₂ = 0.999, are Adam's early steps too large or too small, and why? -> Too large: v's average with β₂ = 0.999 is far more depleted than m's with β₁ = 0.9, so √v underestimates more than m does (a factor 3.16 at t = 1 and about 6.5 near t = 12).
Multiply the loss by 1,000. What happens to the SGD step and to the Adam step? -> SGD's step is 1,000 times larger; Adam's is unchanged, apart from ε.

On the optimiser-paths widget's ravine Adam needs about 126 steps when the valley is aligned with the axes and about 214 when it is rotated by 45°, while gradient descent and heavy ball are unchanged. Why? -> Adam rescales each coordinate separately. Aligned with the axes, that rescaling matches the curvature; rotated, every coordinate mixes the steep and the shallow direction, which no per-coordinate scaling can undo. Gradient descent and momentum act on the gradient vector as a whole, so rotating the problem only rotates their paths.

sections.title: Learning-rate schedules, the range test and gradient clipping
sections.purpose: Set the learning rate over time and find its scale, and guard against gradient spikes, knowing what each device protects against.
must_cover: Why decay, recalled from Module 01 (which derives it; do not re-derive): on one quadratic direction with curvature λ and mini-batch gradient-noise variance s²/B, a constant step leaves the iterate hovering with stationary variance V = ηs²/(Bλ(2 − ηλ)) ≈ ηs²/(2Bλ), an excess loss ½λV proportional to η/B. A constant learning rate therefore leaves the final model at a random point of a band whose width is set by η; decaying η shrinks the band. This is the source's 'the final model is a random point on the oscillation'; what is new here is measuring it on a network (Lab 3) and choosing the schedule.

Schedules: step decay (×0.1 at fixed fractions of training, e.g. 50% and 75%); cosine decay η_t = η_min + ½(η_max − η_min)(1 + cos(πt/T)) (Loshchilov and Hutter 2017); linear warmup from near 0 to η_max over the first T_w steps (typically 1–5% of training, a few hundred to a few thousand steps). Warmup plus cosine to about a tenth of the peak or less is the language-model default; warmup–stable–decay schedules, which hold the peak and decay only at the end, are a common alternative as of 2026 (Module 08).

Why warmup: at the start Adam's v̂ is estimated from a handful of gradients and is noisy even after bias correction, so early steps are erratic (Liu et al. 2020); the curvature at initialisation can be high; and large-batch SGD with a scaled-up learning rate needs a ramp (Goyal et al. 2017, who scale η linearly with the batch size and warm up over 5 epochs). Without warmup a learning rate that is fine later can wreck the first hundred steps.

The peak learning rate is the most important hyperparameter after the architecture (source). The learning-rate range test (Smith 2017): train for a few hundred steps while increasing η geometrically from about 10⁻⁶ to 10, record the loss smoothed by an exponential moving average, and plot it against log η. The loss is flat while η is too small, falls fastest over about a decade, reaches a minimum and then rises steeply. Choose the peak η about 3–10 times below the minimum, near the steepest fall; the full run is longer and noisier than the test.

PyTorch: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max) counts scheduler.step() calls — epochs in the source's loop, batches if stepped per batch; warmup via LinearLR with SequentialLR, or a LambdaLR; call scheduler.step() after optimizer.step().

Gradient clipping by global norm: if ‖g‖ > c over all parameters concatenated, replace g by c·g/‖g‖; the direction is kept. c = 1.0 is common for transformers and recurrent networks (Pascanu et al. 2013; Module 04). Clipping each value separately (clip_grad_value_) changes the direction and is a cruder tool.

Why clipping matters under Adam: the step is normalised, but a single spike still enters m and v. A spike 100 times the typical gradient RMS raises v from 1 to 11 (in units of the typical g²), so √v ≈ 3.3 and every later step of that parameter shrinks about 3.3 times; v relaxes with time constant 1/(1 − β₂) = 1,000 steps and needs about 3,860 steps to return within 10%, while m points along the spike and the next step is about three times the usual size. Clipping before the optimiser prevents both. clip_grad_norm_ returns the pre-clip norm: log it; if clipping fires on most steps, the threshold or the learning rate is wrong.
Batch size and learning rate interact (linear scaling for SGD, Goyal et al. 2017); the large-batch regime belongs to Module 08.
worked_examples: Warmup plus cosine with η_max = 3×10⁻³, η_min = 3×10⁻⁵ (1% of the peak), T = 10,000 steps and T_w = 500 (cosine over the remaining 9,500): η = 1.5×10⁻³ at step 250, 3×10⁻³ at 500, 2.565×10⁻³ at 2,875, 1.515×10⁻³ at 5,250, 4.65×10⁻⁴ at 7,625 and 3×10⁻⁵ at 10,000.

The noise floor, from Module 01's formula with λ = 1 and s²/B = 1: excess loss 0.0263 at η = 0.1 and 0.0025 at η = 0.01, ten times smaller for a ten times smaller η. Lab 3 measures it on a network: for y = sin 3x plus noise of variance 0.0104, SGD with momentum at a constant η = 0.05 ends at a validation MSE of 0.0122 and moves by ±0.0011 between epochs; step decay ends at 0.01044 and warmup + cosine at 0.01041.

Range test on the digits network (Lab 3; 200 steps from 10⁻⁵ to 10): SGD with momentum 0.9 falls fastest near η = 0.055, has its smoothed minimum at 0.29 and diverges by 0.77; Adam falls fastest near 2.3×10⁻³, has its minimum at 0.017 and diverges by 0.059. Chosen peaks: 0.05 for SGD with momentum, 2×10⁻³ for Adam.
Clipping by norm and by value: g = (3, 4) has norm 5; clipping the norm at 1 gives (0.6, 0.8), keeping the direction at 53.1°; clipping each value at 1 gives (1, 1), turning it to 45°.

figures.description: Three schedules over 10,000 steps on one axes (η on a linear y-axis): step decay from 3×10⁻³ with ×0.1 at steps 5,000 and 7,500; cosine from 3×10⁻³ to 3×10⁻⁵ without warmup; a 500-step linear warmup followed by cosine to 3×10⁻⁵. The worked example's values at steps 250, 5,250 and 10,000 are marked.

Range-test curves from Lab 3: smoothed training loss against η on a log x-axis for SGD with momentum and for Adam, each annotated 'too small (flat)', 'steepest fall' (0.055; 2.3×10⁻³) and 'minimum' (0.29; 0.017), each curve cut where it exceeds four times its minimum (0.77; 0.059), and the chosen η marked by a vertical dashed line (0.05; 2×10⁻³).

checks: Why does a constant learning rate leave the final model at 'a random point on the oscillation'? -> With noisy gradients the iterate fluctuates around the minimum with a variance roughly proportional to η; only reducing η reduces the fluctuation.
Gradients (3, 4) are clipped to global norm 1 and, separately, to value 1. Results? -> (0.6, 0.8), same direction; (1, 1), a different direction.
In a range test the loss is lowest at η = 0.1 and explodes at 0.3. What peak learning rate do you choose? -> About 0.01–0.03, a factor 3–10 below the minimum.

sections.title: Normalisation layers
sections.purpose: Explain what batch norm, layer norm and RMSNorm compute, how batch norm behaves differently at training and evaluation time, and why normalisation makes training easier.
must_cover: Batch normalisation (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015), per feature j over the mini-batch: μ_B = (1/B)Σ_i z_ij, σ²_B = (1/B)Σ_i (z_ij − μ_B)², ẑ = (z − μ_B)/√(σ²_B + ε), y = γẑ + β, with learned γ (initialised to 1) and β (initialised to 0) so that the layer can represent any scale and shift, the identity included.

Training against evaluation: in training mode it uses the batch's statistics and updates running averages, μ_run ← (1 − m)μ_run + mμ_B and likewise for the variance (PyTorch: momentum m = 0.1 is the weight of the new value, the opposite convention to an optimiser's momentum; the running variance uses the unbiased batch variance). In evaluation mode (model.eval()) it uses the running averages, so one example's output no longer depends on its batch-mates. Forgetting eval() is a classic bug; so is judging a model early in training, when the running averages still lag the weights.

Consequences (source): an example's output depends on the other examples in its batch; small batches give noisy statistics (below about 16 per batch, group norm or layer norm replace it, Module 03); sequences of varying length fit badly; and in training mode a batch of one has zero variance per feature, which PyTorch refuses with 'Expected more than 1 value per channel when training'.
The bias of the layer in front of a batch norm is redundant (the mean subtraction removes it and β replaces it), hence bias=False in Module 03's code.

Why it helps: the original argument (reducing 'internal covariate shift') has been challenged; Santurkar et al. (2018) found the benefit is mainly a smoother, better-conditioned loss landscape that tolerates larger learning rates. A useful exact fact: batch norm's output is invariant to scaling the weights in front of it (z → cz leaves ẑ unchanged), so the gradient with respect to those weights scales as 1/c and the effective learning rate depends on the weights' norm; weight decay on such weights mostly raises the effective learning rate rather than restricting the function.

Layer normalisation (Ba et al. 2016), per example across its d features: μ = (1/d)Σ_j z_j, σ² = (1/d)Σ_j (z_j − μ)², y = γ ⊙ (z − μ)/√(σ² + ε) + β. Identical in training and evaluation and independent of the batch; used in recurrent networks and transformers.

RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019): y = γ ⊙ z/√(mean(z²) + ε), with no mean subtraction and no β; cheaper, works as well in practice, and is what most large language models use as of 2026. Module 06 places it in the block (pre-norm against post-norm). In PyTorch: nn.BatchNorm1d, nn.LayerNorm and, from version 2.4, nn.RMSNorm.

The backward pass of a normalisation, for layer norm with γ = 1 and ε ignored: from ∂ẑ_k/∂z_j = (𝟙[k = j] − 1/d − ẑ_kẑ_j/d)/σ (four lines from ẑ = (z − μ)/σ, ∂μ/∂z_j = 1/d, ∂σ/∂z_j = ẑ_j/d), ∂𝓛/∂z = (ḡ − mean(ḡ) − ẑ·mean(ḡ ⊙ ẑ))/σ with ḡ = ∂𝓛/∂y. The gradient has zero mean and is orthogonal to ẑ: through a normalisation the network cannot change the mean or the scale of its inputs, only their pattern; γ and β set scale and offset.
worked_examples: Layer norm and RMSNorm by hand for z = (1, 2, 3, 6), γ = 1, β = 0, ε = 0: mean 3, deviations (−2, −1, 0, 3), variance 14/4 = 3.5, standard deviation 1.871, layer-norm output (−1.069, −0.535, 0, 1.604); RMS √(50/4) = 3.536, RMSNorm output (0.283, 0.566, 0.849, 1.697), whose mean is 0.849 (not centred) and whose RMS is 1.

Batch norm on one feature over a batch of four, z = (2, 4, 6, 8): μ_B = 5, σ²_B = 5, training-mode output (−1.342, −0.447, 0.447, 1.342). After this one step the running statistics, starting from (0, 1) with m = 0.1, are mean 0.5 and variance 0.9·1 + 0.1·(20/3) = 1.567 (the unbiased variance is 6.667). An input of 6 is normalised to 0.447 in training mode but to (6 − 0.5)/√1.567 = 4.394 in evaluation mode: why evaluation numbers early in training can look wrong. All four numbers are what torch.nn.BatchNorm1d returns.
A zero-variance feature: if every example in the batch has the same value in one feature, batch norm outputs exactly 0 for it (ε keeps the division finite) — compare the constant pixels of Lab 4.

sections.title: Regularisation for networks
sections.purpose: Cover the regularisers specific to training networks — weight decay, dropout, early stopping, augmentation, label smoothing — with what each does to the gradient and when each fails.
must_cover: Recall Module 01: regularisation trades variance for bias and is tuned on the validation set. Networks are routinely over-parameterised (Lab 4 fits 26,122 parameters to 1,078 training images) and still generalise, partly through the implicit regularisation of SGD noise (Module 01) and partly through the explicit methods below.
Weight decay via AdamW (s8): typical λ from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻¹ depending on the optimiser and its convention; excluded from biases and normalisation gains; its interaction with normalisation (s10).

Dropout (Srivastava et al. 2014): during training multiply each hidden unit by an independent mask m_i ~ Bernoulli(1 − p) and by 1/(1 − p) (inverted dropout); at evaluation do nothing. Derive E[h̃_i] = (1 − p)·h_i/(1 − p) + p·0 = h_i, so the next layer sees the same expected input in both modes; derive Var(h̃_i) = h_i²·p/(1 − p), i.e. multiplicative noise (relative variance 1 at p = 0.5, 0.11 at p = 0.1). The original formulation scaled the weights by (1 − p) at test time instead; frameworks implement the inverted form.

Why it works: the network cannot rely on any single unit, and training samples from 2^n thinned networks that share weights. At evaluation the full, scaled network approximates their ensemble — exactly, for a single layer feeding a softmax, the renormalised geometric mean of the sub-networks' predictions (Hinton et al. 2012); approximately for deeper networks. Keeping dropout on at test time and averaging many passes gives a cheap uncertainty estimate (Monte Carlo dropout, Gal and Ghahramani 2016).

Typical p: up to 0.5 in older MLPs and AlexNet's fully connected layers; 0.1 in transformers; many large language model pretraining runs use none, because each token is seen about once (as of 2026; Module 08).

Early stopping: evaluate the validation loss every epoch, keep the best checkpoint, stop after a patience of several epochs without improvement. Recall Module 01's filter factors (do not re-derive): t steps of gradient descent from zero leave eigen-direction i at [1 − (1 − ηλ_i)^t]θ*_i, close to ridge regression's λ_i/(λ_i + α)·θ*_i with α ≈ 1/(ηt), so early stopping is approximately L2 regularisation whose strength is set by the training time (Goodfellow et al. 2016, §7.8). What is new for networks is the procedure: checkpoints, patience, and restoring the best weights.

Calibration, which Module 01 measures and defers here for networks: networks trained long with cross-entropy tend to be overconfident. Temperature scaling (Guo et al. 2017) divides the logits by one scalar T > 0 fitted on the validation set by minimising the negative log-likelihood; it changes confidence but not the argmax, so accuracy is untouched. Label smoothing acts at training time instead and can overshoot into underconfidence, which a temperature then undoes. Module 07 returns to calibration for language models.

Data augmentation: label-preserving transformations add data the model must be invariant to; for images it is the most effective regulariser (Module 03); for sensor or tabular data, input noise (training with Gaussian input noise is equivalent to a Tikhonov penalty to first order, Bishop 1995), and time shifts or scalings to which the label really is invariant.

Label smoothing (Szegedy et al. 2016): train on y_LS = (1 − α)y + α/K; the gradient with respect to the logits becomes p̂ − y_LS. With hard labels, cross-entropy on separable data keeps pushing the logit margin towards infinity; with smoothing the optimum has the finite log-odds margin ln((1 − α + α/K)/(α/K)). It often improves calibration and accuracy but erases information that knowledge distillation would use (Müller et al. 2019). PyTorch: F.cross_entropy(..., label_smoothing=α).
Above all, more data (source): a network's variance falls with N and no regulariser substitutes for it. Every regulariser changes the best learning rate; re-tune η after adding one.
worked_examples: Inverted dropout with p = 0.5 on h = (2.0, 0.5, 1.0, 3.0) and mask (1, 0, 1, 0): h̃ = (4.0, 0, 2.0, 0); averaged over all masks, h̃ equals h. With p = 0.1 the survivors are scaled by 1.111.

Label smoothing with α = 0.1 and K = 10: targets 0.91 for the true class and 0.01 for each other class; optimal logit gap ln(0.91/0.01) = ln 91 = 4.51. For a confident prediction p̂_true = 0.999 (others 0.000111): hard labels give δ_true = −0.001 (keep pushing); smoothing gives δ_true = 0.999 − 0.91 = +0.089 and δ_other = −0.0099 (pull back).

Early stopping as L2: η = 0.01 and t = 1,000 steps correspond roughly to a ridge strength α ≈ 1/(ηt) = 0.1. Lab 4 measures early stopping on digits: the validation loss is lowest at epoch 29 (0.1145) while the training loss keeps falling to 0.002, and the run stops at epoch 44 with a patience of 15.

Temperature scaling on Lab 4's model (seed 0, best checkpoint; T fitted by a grid search over [0.05, 5] on the validation NLL): T = 1.20, a mildly overconfident model; test NLL 0.134 → 0.124, expected calibration error 0.013 → 0.012, accuracy unchanged at 96.9%. The same network trained with label smoothing 0.1 is underconfident — mean top probability 0.865 at 98.3% test accuracy, calibration error 0.118 — and its fitted T = 0.49 brings the calibration error to 0.012 and the test NLL from 0.175 to 0.057. (One seed each: the 1.4-point accuracy difference is about 1.5 times the 0.9-point standard error of a single test accuracy — not a finding.)

sections.title: Losses and numerical stability
sections.purpose: Compute losses so that nothing overflows or underflows, and know the floating-point formats well enough to predict where training will break.
must_cover: Floating-point formats with their sign/exponent/mantissa bits: fp32 (1/8/23): largest 3.40×10³⁸, smallest normal 1.18×10⁻³⁸, smallest subnormal 1.4×10⁻⁴⁵, machine epsilon 1.19×10⁻⁷; bf16 (1/8/7): the range of fp32 (largest 3.39×10³⁸) but epsilon 7.8×10⁻³, two to three significant digits; fp16 (1/5/10): largest 65,504, smallest normal 6.1×10⁻⁵, smallest subnormal 6×10⁻⁸, epsilon 9.8×10⁻⁴. Hence e^z overflows fp32 and bf16 above z ≈ 88.7 and fp16 above z ≈ 11.09; e^(−z) underflows to zero in fp32 beyond z ≈ 103 and in fp16 beyond z ≈ 16.6.

Derive the log-sum-exp identity: Σ_j e^(z_j) = e^m Σ_j e^(z_j − m) for any m, so log Σ_j e^(z_j) = m + log Σ_j e^(z_j − m) — Module 01's observation that adding a constant to every logit changes nothing, put to work. With m = max_j z_j every exponent is ≤ 0 (no overflow) and one term equals 1, so the sum is ≥ 1 (no log 0). Module 01's stable binary form, softplus(z) − yz with softplus(z) = max(z, 0) + ln(1 + e^(−|z|)), is the K = 2 case.
Cross-entropy from logits: ℓ = logsumexp(z) − z_y, and log_softmax(z) = z − logsumexp(z). The fused function (F.cross_entropy on logits) computes both the loss and its gradient p̂ − y stably.

Why never log(softmax(z)) in two steps: softmax can underflow to exactly 0 for a very negative logit, and log 0 = −∞ gives an infinite loss and NaN gradients, while log_softmax returns the finite value. And never apply a softmax before F.cross_entropy, which applies log-softmax itself: the network's probabilities become logits confined to [0, 1], the loss cannot fall below −ln(e/(e + K − 1)), and the gradients are small, so learning is very slow (source: 'a common, silent bug').

The binary case: BCEWithLogitsLoss computes ℓ = max(z, 0) − zy + log(1 + e^(−|z|)) from the logit. A sigmoid followed by BCELoss saturates: in fp32 σ(z) rounds to exactly 1.0 from z ≈ 16.7, log(1 − 1) = −∞, and PyTorch clamps the log at −100, so the loss is silently capped at 100 and its gradient is wrong.

Regression (source): squared error punishes outliers quadratically (Module 01: it is the Gaussian negative log-likelihood); the Huber loss, ½r² for |r| ≤ δ and δ(|r| − δ/2) beyond, has its gradient clipped at ±δ and is the usual compromise; absolute error corresponds to Laplace noise.

Reduction: a mean over the batch keeps the gradient's scale independent of B; a sum multiplies it, and so the effective learning rate, by B. PyTorch's default is the mean; stay consistent when changing the batch size.

Mixed precision in one paragraph (depth in Module 08): compute matrix products in bf16 or fp16 but keep master weights, softmax, losses and normalisation statistics in fp32 (torch.autocast does the latter automatically). fp16 also needs loss scaling — multiply the loss by S (e.g. 2¹⁶) before backward and divide the gradients by S — so that small gradients do not underflow (Micikevicius et al. 2018); bf16 has fp32's range and needs none, which is why the source's advice for NaN losses is 'use bf16 rather than fp16'.
Compute variances as mean((x − μ)²), not mean(x²) − μ², which cancels catastrophically in low precision.
worked_examples: Logits z = (1000, 999, 998), target class 0. Naive: e¹⁰⁰⁰ is inf in float64 and inf/inf is NaN. Stable: m = 1000, Σ e^(z − m) = 1 + e⁻¹ + e⁻² = 1.50321, logsumexp = 1000.40761, loss 0.40761 (F.cross_entropy returns 0.407606).

Underflow in log(softmax): for z = (0, −120) in fp32, softmax gives (1, 0) because e⁻¹²⁰ = 7.7×10⁻⁵³ is below the smallest subnormal; taking the log gives (0, −inf), while log_softmax gives (0, −120).

The softmax-before-cross-entropy floor: at best the true class gets probability 1, which as a logit gives p̂_y = e/(e + K − 1), so the loss cannot fall below 1.461 for K = 10, 0.313 for K = 2, 3.622 for K = 100 and 5.909 for K = 1,000. Lab 5's script A plateaus at 1.469.
Sigmoid saturation: in fp32 σ(16.6) = 0.99999988 but σ(16.7) = 1.0 exactly; for z = 17 and y = 0, BCELoss on σ(z) returns 100 (the clamp) while BCEWithLogitsLoss returns the correct 17.0.
fp16 overflow: np.exp(np.float16(11)) = 59,870 but np.exp(np.float16(12)) = inf (ln 65,504 = 11.09).

figures.description: Three horizontal number lines on a common log scale from 10⁻⁴⁶ to 10³⁹, one per format (fp32, bf16, fp16), each with ticks at the smallest subnormal, the smallest normal and the largest value, and the machine epsilon written beside the format's name. Vertical markers show e^z at the overflow thresholds (z = 88.7 for fp32 and bf16; z = 11.09 for fp16) and the value 65,504.

Why can bf16 hold e⁸⁰ while fp16 cannot hold e¹²? -> bf16 has fp32's 8 exponent bits (largest value about 3.4×10³⁸); fp16 has 5 (largest 65,504 ≈ e^11.09).

Source §9's NaN advice (check the log-sum-exp; use bf16 rather than fp16) and source Exercise 5, which becomes e11.

sections.title: A complete training loop
sections.purpose: Put every piece of the module into one short PyTorch training loop and say which section justifies each line, so that the loop can be read rather than copied.
must_cover: Reproduce the source's §10 loop unchanged: torch.manual_seed(0); 2,048 points uniform in the square [−1, 1]² with label 1 inside the circle x₁² + x₂² < 0.5; the first 1,536 for training and the last 512 for validation; standardisation with the training mean and standard deviation; a 2 → 32 → 32 → 2 MLP with GELU; AdamW (lr 3×10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻²); CosineAnnealingLR with T_max = 400; 400 epochs of shuffled mini-batches of 64; F.cross_entropy on the logits; zero_grad, backward, clip_grad_norm_ at 1.0, step; one scheduler step per epoch; every 100 epochs model.eval() and torch.no_grad() to print the last batch's loss and the validation accuracy.

Annotate every line with its justification: the seed (reproducibility; report the spread over seeds, s14); training-statistics standardisation (Module 01, leakage); GELU (s5); the default initialisation (s6: adequate at this depth); AdamW and its decoupled decay (s8); the cosine schedule (s9); F.cross_entropy on logits (s12); zero_grad before backward (s4); clipping (s9); model.train()/model.eval() (s10, s11 — this model has no dropout or batch norm, but the habit costs nothing); torch.no_grad() at evaluation (s4).

Two reading notes: the printed loss is the last mini-batch's loss, which is noisy (0.0069, 0.0205, 0.0056, 0.0107 at epochs 100–400) — log the epoch mean instead; and T_max counts scheduler.step() calls, here epochs.

The same model written as an nn.Module subclass — __init__ creates the layers as attributes, forward composes them — in six lines. Lab 4 writes its model this way, and Module 03's residual Block and SmallResNet build on exactly this form.

The baseline that gives the number its meaning: logistic regression on the same standardised inputs reaches 59.2% validation accuracy, exactly the majority-class rate, because a line cannot separate a disc from its complement.
worked_examples: Outputs (seed 0, laptop CPU with 4 threads, about 26 s): epoch 100 — last-batch loss 0.0069, validation accuracy 0.992; epoch 200 — 0.0205, 0.996; epoch 300 — 0.0056, 0.996; epoch 400 — 0.0107, 0.996. Over seeds 0–4 the final validation accuracies are 0.9961, 0.9980, 0.9922, 0.9980 and 1.0000: mean 99.69%, standard deviation 0.30 points (the source's 'about 99%' and 'a fraction of a percent'). The positive class is 40.7% of the training points (the disc covers π·0.5/4 = 39.3% of the square).

Left: the 512 validation points coloured by class, the trained network's decision boundary drawn as the contour p̂ = 0.5 (a near-circle) and the true circle of radius √0.5 dashed. Right: the same points with the logistic-regression boundary (a straight line, or none inside the square) and '59.2% = majority class' noted.

The printed loss jumps from 0.0069 at epoch 100 to 0.0205 at epoch 200. Is training going wrong? -> No: it is a single mini-batch's loss; the epoch mean and the validation accuracy (0.992 → 0.996) are the signals.

sections.title: Training dynamics and debugging
sections.purpose: Turn a misbehaving run into a diagnosis: what to test before training, what to watch during it, how to read the curves, and a checklist to work through.
must_cover: Before training, four cheap tests. (1) The initial loss: a network with small random weights predicts near-uniform probabilities, so the initial cross-entropy is about ln K (2.303 for 10 classes; Lab 4 measures 2.309); far above it means the initial scale is wrong (Lab 5's 𝒩(0, 1) initialisation starts at 677). For regression with a near-zero initial output, the initial MSE is about the mean of the squared targets. (2) Overfit one batch: 8–32 examples should be driven to near-zero loss within a few hundred steps; if not, the pipeline is broken, and no amount of data will help (source). (3) Gradient-check every hand-written or custom component (below). (4) Look at the data: a few inputs with their labels, class counts, ranges, NaNs and zero-variance features.

Gradient checking done properly: the central difference (𝓛(θ + ε) − 𝓛(θ − ε))/(2ε) has truncation error ≈ 𝓛'''ε²/6 and rounding error ≈ u|𝓛|/ε, minimised near ε = (3u)^(1/3): about 10⁻⁵ in float64 (u = 1.1×10⁻¹⁶, error about 10⁻¹¹) but about 5×10⁻³ in float32 (error about 10⁻⁵), so check in float64. Compare with the relative error |a − n|/max(10⁻⁸, |a| + |n|): below 10⁻⁷ passes; 10⁻⁴ or more is a bug unless a kink is involved. ReLU kinks cause false alarms when a pre-activation lies within ε of zero (Lab 1 finds one at 2×10⁻⁷). Check several entries of every tensor. torch.autograd.gradcheck does all this for any function of double-precision inputs (defaults eps = 10⁻⁶, atol = 10⁻⁵, rtol = 10⁻³).

During training, log and plot on shared x-axes: the training loss (epoch mean, log scale), the validation loss and metric every epoch, the learning rate, and the global gradient norm before clipping (source: 'most stories are visible in those three lines'). Per layer, with forward hooks: activation standard deviation, fraction of dead ReLU units, gradient norm, and the update-to-weight ratio ‖Δθ‖/‖θ‖ measured from the actual parameter change (a common rule of thumb is about 10⁻³; under AdamW at 10⁻³ Lab 4 sees about 10⁻² in epoch 1, 2×10⁻³ at epoch 10 and 2.5×10⁻⁴ at epoch 30).

Reading the curves (the source's list, extended): loss flat from the start → learning rate far too small, or no gradient (a bug, a detached tensor, dead units, labels misaligned with inputs); loss NaN → learning rate too large or an overflow (s12): lower η, add warmup, clip, compute from logits, use bf16 not fp16, and torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) to find the first bad operation; loss falls then spikes or climbs → learning rate too high late in training, missing warmup, a bad batch, or accumulating gradients (missing zero_grad); training falls while validation rises → overfitting (s11); both plateau high → underfitting, or a learning rate that decayed too early (a bigger model, a longer schedule); validation loss below training loss → dropout or augmentation active only in training (normal), or leakage; training loss stuck near 1.46 for 10 classes → softmax before the loss; loss falling but accuracy flat → class imbalance or a metric bug.

Noise in the measurement: a test accuracy p on n examples has standard error √(p(1 − p)/n); for p = 0.97 and n = 360 that is 0.009, so two runs one point apart are not distinguishable. Seed-to-seed spread is a separate source of variation (Lab 4: 97.39% ± 0.32 over five seeds). Report both, and the baseline.

The checklist, in order: 1 look at the data; 2 standardise with training statistics and guard zero variances; 3 check shapes through the model, and targets against outputs; 4 check the initial loss; 5 gradient-check custom code in float64; 6 overfit one batch; 7 train while logging loss, validation, learning rate and gradient norm; 8 watch the per-layer statistics; 9 compare against a baseline; 10 evaluate under model.eval() and torch.no_grad(), touch the test set once, and report its standard error and the seed spread.
worked_examples: The initial-loss check on digits (Lab 4): 2.309 against ln 10 = 2.303; with every weight drawn from 𝒩(0, 1) instead (Lab 5, script C): 677.
Overfitting one batch (Lab 4): 32 digits, AdamW at 10⁻³ without decay: loss 2.31 at step 0, 0.046 at step 50, 0.0037 at 100, 0.0012 at 200.
The gradient-check error budget in float64 with 𝓛 ≈ 1: at ε = 10⁻¹² the rounding error is about 10⁻¹⁶/10⁻¹² = 10⁻⁴, far worse than at ε = 10⁻⁵ (truncation about 2×10⁻¹¹, rounding about 10⁻¹¹).

Lab 4's per-layer monitoring at epochs 1, 10 and 30: activation standard deviation of the two hidden layers 0.37/0.22 → 0.62/1.01 → 0.68/1.24; dead fraction 0/0.008 → 0/0.016 → 0/0.016; full-batch gradient norms of the three weight matrices 0.25/0.32/0.39 → 0.029/0.020/0.042 → 0.004/0.003/0.005. Nothing needs action: this is what a healthy run looks like.
Standard error: a test accuracy of 0.9694 on 360 images is ±0.0091 (Lab 4, seed 0).

figures.description: A 2 × 2 grid of representative training and validation loss curves on log y-axes, each with a thin gradient-norm trace on a twin axis: (a) healthy — both fall, validation flattens, the gradient norm decays; (b) learning rate too high — the loss falls, spikes, then becomes NaN (marked with a cross), the gradient norm spiking first; (c) overfitting — training keeps falling while validation turns up at a marked epoch; (d) no learning — flat at ln 10 = 2.30 with a gradient norm near zero. Each panel is titled with its diagnosis and first fix.

checks: A new 10-class model starts training at a loss of 47. What do you suspect before anything else? -> The initial weights or output scale are too large: a sensible initialisation starts near ln 10 = 2.30.
Two configurations score 97.2% and 97.8% on 360 test images. Is the second better? -> Not shown: the standard error is about 0.9 points, and the seed spread adds more.
Why compute gradient checks in float64? -> In float32 the best attainable central-difference accuracy is about 10⁻⁵ even for a correct gradient, too coarse to separate bugs from rounding.
