sections.new_material: The initial-loss test with measured values; gradient-check error analysis (optimal ε, float64, relative-error thresholds, kinks); per-layer monitoring with hooks and the measured update-to-weight ratio; more curve signatures; the standard error of a test metric and the seed spread; the ordered checklist.

what_goes_wrong: Training loss sits near ln K (2.30 for 10 classes) from the first step -> no gradient reaches the weights: a detached tensor or requires_grad=False, all ReLU units dead, labels shuffled independently of their inputs, or a learning rate near zero -> overfit one batch of 32; print per-layer gradient norms; check that loss.grad_fn is not None; look at a few (input, label) pairs.

Training loss plateaus near 1.46 on a 10-class problem (0.31 on a 2-class one) while accuracy looks reasonable -> a softmax is applied before F.cross_entropy, so probabilities are treated as logits and the loss cannot fall below −ln(e/(e + K − 1)) -> pass the raw logits to the loss (Lab 5, script A: 1.469 after 20 epochs).

The initial loss is far above ln K (677 instead of 2.30 in Lab 5) -> the initial weights are too large (𝒩(0, 1) instead of He or the framework default), so the logits are huge and confidently wrong -> use a variance-preserving initialisation and check the initial loss before training (s6, s14).

The loss becomes NaN or inf after some steps -> the learning rate is too high, or something overflows (exp of large logits, fp16 above 65,504), takes log(0) or divides by a zero standard deviation -> lower η or add warmup, clip the global gradient norm at 1.0, compute losses from logits, prefer bf16 to fp16, guard divisions; torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) names the first bad operation.

The loss falls, then rises and wanders while the gradient norm grows every epoch (7 → 194 in Lab 5) -> optimizer.zero_grad() is missing, so .grad accumulates across steps -> zero the gradients before every backward pass.

Validation accuracy differs between two evaluations of the same weights, or depends on the evaluation batch size (92.2% and 93.0% in train mode, 84.4% in batches of 8, against 96.7% in eval mode in Lab 5) -> model.eval() was forgotten, so dropout masks and batch-norm batch statistics are active -> evaluate under model.eval() and torch.no_grad(), and call model.train() before training resumes.

Batch norm with a batch of one raises 'Expected more than 1 value per channel when training', and with batches of two or four training is noisy and evaluation disagrees with training -> batch statistics are undefined or meaningless for tiny batches -> use layer norm, RMSNorm or group norm, or larger batches.

The final loss jitters from epoch to epoch and ends well above the noise floor (Lab 3: validation MSE 0.0122 against a floor of 0.0104) -> a constant learning rate: SGD noise holds the iterate in a band whose width grows with η -> decay the learning rate (cosine or step) so the run settles; the final model is otherwise a random point on the oscillation.

A custom layer or hand-written backward pass 'trains', but one part never improves -> a wrong or missing gradient (a forgotten gate, a wrong transpose, a stray detach) -> compare with central finite differences in float64 (relative error below 10⁻⁷), allowing for ReLU kinks and near-zero gradients.

A deep plain network (twenty sigmoid layers) does not train with any optimiser -> vanishing gradients: every layer multiplies the error by σ' ≤ 1/4 -> change the architecture, not the optimiser: ReLU-family activations, He initialisation, normalisation, residual connections.

Activations shrink to the level of the biases (standard deviation about 0.04) or blow up through depth at initialisation -> the initial scale does not preserve variance; PyTorch's nn.Linear default, U(±1/√n_in), shrinks a ReLU signal's second moment 6× per layer -> use He initialisation for deep ReLU stacks and log per-layer activation statistics at step 0.

A regression loss stalls at exactly the variance of the targets and the predictions are constant -> targets of shape (B,) against predictions of shape (B, 1) broadcast to a (B, B) difference matrix whose mean is minimised by predicting the mean -> make the shapes equal (squeeze or unsqueeze) and treat PyTorch's broadcasting warning as an error.

Weight decay tuned with Adam(weight_decay=λ) behaves inconsistently across layers and must be re-tuned whenever the learning rate changes -> coupled L2: the decay term is divided by √v̂, so it is weak where gradients are large -> use AdamW (decoupled decay) and exclude biases and normalisation gains from decay.

Validation statistics leak into input standardisation, or a constant feature divides by zero (four always-zero pixels in load_digits give 1,436 NaNs in the validation set) -> the mean and standard deviation were computed on the wrong split, or a standard deviation is 0 -> compute them on the training split only and replace zero standard deviations by 1.

labs.title: Backpropagation by hand in NumPy
labs.goal: Implement the forward and backward pass of a two-layer MLP in NumPy, verify every gradient entry against finite differences, cross-check against PyTorch, train it on y = sin 3x, and see what the initial scale does to training.
labs.data: Synthetic: 256 training points x ~ U(−1, 1) with t = sin 3x, then 1,000 validation points from the same distribution, drawn with numpy.random.default_rng(1) in the order X, T, initial parameters, validation set, so that training reproduces the source's code exactly.
steps: Set-up: copy the source's init, forward and backward functions unchanged (W1 from 𝒩(0, 2/1), W2 from 𝒩(0, 1/64), zero biases; ReLU; mean squared error with dY = 2(Y − T)/B). Draw X (256, 1) and T, then p = init(1, 64, 1), then the validation set (1,000 points). Print the shapes of X, Z1, H1 and Y for the batch — (256, 1), (256, 64), (256, 64), (256, 1) — and the initial training MSE, 0.3270 (the mean of T² is 0.549).

Gradient check of all 193 entries with central differences in float64 at ε = 10⁻⁵, printing the worst relative error |a − n|/max(10⁻⁸, |a| + |n|) per tensor: W1 5.1×10⁻⁹, b1 7.9×10⁻⁴, W2 1.3×10⁻⁸, b2 6.3×10⁻¹². About 0.04 s.

Investigate the one entry that looks bad: find the b1 unit with the worst error (unit 55) and print the smallest |z| over the batch for that unit, 2.0×10⁻⁷ — inside ±ε, so the difference quotient straddles the ReLU kink. Repeat with ε = 10⁻⁷: worst b1 error 1.7×10⁻⁷. A comment records the conclusion: a kink, not a bug.

Break the backward pass on purpose (drop the ReLU gate: dZ1 = dH1) and rerun the check: W1 0.38, b1 1.0, while W2 and b2 stay at 1.3×10⁻⁸ and 6.3×10⁻¹² — the check points at the layer below the missing gate. Restore the code.

Cross-check with PyTorch at the initial parameters: build nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 1)).double(), print its weight shapes, (64, 1) and (1, 64), copy W1.T, b1, W2.T and b2 into it, compute the same loss and call backward. The losses agree to 16 digits (0.32700646052813…) and the largest gradient difference is about 2×10⁻¹⁶. Then run torch.autograd.gradcheck on a small double-precision function (the sum of ReLU of a 4×3 by 3×2 product): True.

Train with 3,000 full-batch gradient-descent steps at η = 0.05, printing the training MSE every 500 steps: 0.327, 0.0204, 0.00488, 0.00164, 0.000774, 0.000439; final training MSE 2.81×10⁻⁴ and validation MSE 3.67×10⁻⁴ (about 0.5 s). Print the number of hidden units never active on the training set (1) and the MSE on [1, 2], outside the training range: 0.403.

Initialisation comparison (the source's Exercise 2), over 10 initialisation seeds (numpy.random.default_rng(100 + s)) with the same data, for He, 𝒩(0, 1) and 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴) (standard deviation 0.01) in both layers; print medians and ranges and plot the median loss curves on a log scale (about 11 s). Expected: He — initial loss median 0.72 (range 0.19–2.0), step 100 median 0.10, final median 3.5×10⁻⁴; 𝒩(0, 1) — initial median 7.9 (range 0.32–24), step 100 median 0.015, final median 2.3×10⁻⁴; 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴) — initial 0.549 for every seed, still 0.114 at step 1,000, final median 9.0×10⁻³, about 25 times worse than He.
expected_observations: Finite differences and backpropagation agree to 10⁻⁸ or better except where a pre-activation lies within ε of a ReLU kink: a gradient check is only as good as its ε and the smoothness of the function.
Removing the ReLU gate corrupts only the gradients of W1 and b1: the check localises the bug to a layer.
PyTorch's autograd computes exactly the four equations of s3; the only difference is the stored weight layout, (out, in).
The training error falls by three orders of magnitude, but the fitted function is good only inside the data's range: outside it the ReLU network extrapolates linearly (MSE 0.403 on [1, 2]).

With 𝒩(0, 1) the initial loss is large and varies by a factor of 75 between seeds, because at initialisation this zero-bias network is just two random straight lines; it is shallow, so it recovers. With 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴) each layer's gradient is proportional to the other layer's tiny weights, so training sits on a plateau near 0.11 for about a thousand steps before escaping. In a deep network both effects compound layer by layer (s6's table; extension 2).
extensions: Replace ReLU by tanh in forward and backward (φ' = 1 − H1²), rerun the gradient check and the training, and compare the final error.

Generalise forward and backward to L layers with loops over lists of weight matrices, gradient-check them, and repeat step 7 with five hidden layers of 64 units: 𝒩(0, 1) now explodes and 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴) stalls.

Engineering variant: fit the neo-Hookean nominal stress P = 2c₁(λ − λ⁻²) of Module 01 (c₁ = 0.5 MPa, stretches λ from 0.6 to 1.0, 2% noise) with this network, and compare its prediction at λ = 0.5 with the one-parameter physical model's.
Switch to mini-batches of 32 and compare the loss curves with full-batch training at the same number of epochs.

labs.title: A scalar autodiff engine in about 100 lines
labs.goal: Build reverse-mode automatic differentiation from scratch — a Value class that records the graph and back-propagates adjoints — verify it by hand, against finite differences and against PyTorch, and use it to train a small MLP.
labs.data: scikit-learn's make_moons, generated locally with no download: 100 training points (noise 0.1, random_state 0) and 500 test points (noise 0.1, random_state 1).
steps: Write class Value with the fields data, grad, _parents and _local (the local partial derivative with respect to each parent, computed during the forward pass) and __slots__ for speed. Operations: +, *, ** (constant exponent), unary −, −, / (through ** −1), exp, log, sin, tanh and relu; each returns a new Value recording its parents and local derivatives, and plain Python numbers are wrapped automatically (__radd__, __rmul__).

Write backward(): an iterative depth-first topological sort (no recursion, so long graphs do not hit Python's recursion limit), then self.grad = 1 and, for each node in reverse order, parent.grad += node.grad × local derivative (the chain rule summed over paths). Return the number of nodes.

Verify on s4's example f = ln x₁ + x₁x₂ − sin x₂ at (2, 5): print f = 11.6521, ∂f/∂x₁ = 5.5000 and ∂f/∂x₂ = 1.7163 (9 nodes, counting the constant −1 created by the subtraction), and check both against central differences.
Build the Neuron (He-initialised weights drawn with random.gauss, zero bias, optional ReLU), Layer and MLP classes; create MLP(2, [16, 16, 1]) after random.seed(0) and print its parameter count, 337.

Loss: the mean binary cross-entropy from logits in the stable form relu(z) − z·y + log(1 + exp(−|z|)) with |z| = relu(z) + relu(−z), built from the engine's own primitives (s12). Train for 100 steps of full-batch gradient descent at η = 1.0, zeroing every grad before backward, and print every 20 steps the loss, the training accuracy and the graph size: step 0 — 1.065, 0.29, 66,440 nodes; step 20 — 0.198, 0.92; step 40 — 0.197, 0.96; step 60 — 0.131, 0.97; step 80 — 0.074, 0.98; step 100 — 0.035, 0.99. About 60 s.
Evaluate on the 500 test points with a plain-float forward pass (no graph): accuracy about 0.99. Plot the decision boundary on a 100 × 100 grid with the same float forward pass.

Cross-check against PyTorch: copy the trained weights into float64 tensors, compute the same loss with F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits and call backward. The losses agree to ten decimal places (0.0295951652) and the largest gradient difference is about 10⁻¹⁶.

Time one forward and backward pass of the engine (about 0.36 s) against the vectorised PyTorch version after a warm-up (about 0.5 ms) and print the ratio, about 700: the engine creates 66,440 Python objects per step, where PyTorch runs about ten tensor operations.
expected_observations: Reverse mode takes a few dozen lines once each primitive knows its local derivative; the '+=' accumulation is what handles variables used more than once.
The engine's gradients equal PyTorch's to machine precision: autograd frameworks do the same thing, on tensors.
Memory and time grow with the number of graph nodes (66,440 for 100 examples through 337 parameters): the tape is reverse mode's price (s4).

The initial loss is 1.06, above ln 2 = 0.69, because the output neuron also uses He initialisation and its logits start large; s14's initial-loss check would flag this, and a smaller output initialisation fixes it.
With η = 1.0 the network fits the moons in 100 steps; with η = 0.5 for 50 steps and then 0.1 it stalls near 92% at step 100 — the learning rate matters even for a toy (s9).
extensions: Add a softplus primitive and a tanh option for the hidden layers, and compare the training curves.
Add forward mode: give Value a tangent field propagated by every operation, and compute ∂f/∂x₁ of the s4 example in one forward pass.
Support a Value exponent in ** (x**y) and check the gradient with respect to both arguments by finite differences.
Write a micro tensor version in which data is a NumPy array and each operation stores a VJP function instead of scalar local derivatives; time it against the scalar engine.

labs.title: Optimisers, schedules and the range test
labs.goal: Find learning rates with a range test, compare SGD, momentum, Nesterov, Adam and AdamW on the same network and data, measure what a schedule does to the noise floor, and verify Adam's sign-like first step.
labs.data: load_digits from scikit-learn (1,797 8×8 images shipped with the package), split 60/20/20 stratified with random_state 0 into 1,078/359/360 and standardised with training statistics (zero standard deviations replaced by 1), for parts 1, 2, 3 and 5; a synthetic regression y = sin 3x + 0.1ε with 4,096 training and 2,048 validation points (torch.manual_seed(0)) for part 4.
steps: Shared set-up: load, split and standardise digits; make(seed) returns the 64 → 128 → 128 → 10 ReLU MLP with PyTorch's default initialisation under torch.manual_seed(seed); evaluate(model, X, y) returns the loss and accuracy under model.eval() and torch.no_grad().

Range test (s9): 200 steps with η growing geometrically from 10⁻⁵ to 10, mini-batches of 64 cycled through the training set, the loss smoothed by an exponential moving average (factor 0.9, bias-corrected), stopping when the smoothed loss exceeds four times its minimum. Print, for SGD with momentum 0.9: steepest fall near η = 0.055, minimum 0.311 at η ≈ 0.29, stopped at η ≈ 0.77 (step 163); for Adam: steepest fall near 2.3×10⁻³, minimum 0.230 at ≈ 0.017, stopped at ≈ 0.059 (step 126). Plot both curves (fig-02-16). About 4 s.

Shoot-out: train for 20 epochs from the same initialisation (seed 0) and batch order with SGD at η = 0.05, SGD at η = 0.5, SGD + momentum 0.9 at η = 0.05, Nesterov at η = 0.05, Adam at 2×10⁻³ and AdamW at 2×10⁻³ with weight decay 10⁻². Print a table with the first epoch whose full training loss is below 0.1, the final training loss, and the validation loss and accuracy. Expected: SGD 0.05 — never (final loss 0.129, validation accuracy 94.2%); SGD 0.5 — epoch 3 (0.0027, 97.5%); momentum — epoch 3 (0.0024, 97.2%); Nesterov — epoch 3 (0.0025, 97.2%); Adam — epoch 4 (0.0018, 96.4%); AdamW — epoch 4 (0.0019, 96.4%). Plot the training loss against step on a log scale. About 12 s.

Schedules on the noisy regression: a 1 → 64 → 64 → 1 ReLU MLP trained with SGD + momentum 0.9 at peak η = 0.05, batch 32, for 20 epochs (2,560 steps) under three schedules: constant; step (×0.1 at 50% and ×0.01 at 75% of the steps); 5% linear warmup then cosine to 0. Print the noise floor (the validation MSE of the true function, 0.0104) and, per schedule, the final validation MSE and the standard deviation of the last five epochs' validation MSE: constant 0.0122 (±0.0011); step 0.01044 (±0.00001); cosine 0.01041 (±0.00003). About 25 s.

Adam's first step: from a fresh model take one Adam step (η = 10⁻³) on the first training batch; print the number of parameters with zero gradient (786), the range of the non-zero gradient magnitudes (1.1×10⁻⁸ to 4.4×10⁻²) and the fraction of those parameters that moved by more than 0.99η (0.9988).
expected_observations: The range test finds the right decade in seconds; Adam's usable range sits 13 to 25 times below that of SGD with momentum (steepest fall 2.3×10⁻³ against 0.055; divergence 0.059 against 0.77).
Momentum with η = 0.05 behaves like plain SGD with η = 0.5: its effective learning rate is η/(1 − μ) (s7).

Adam is not faster than well-tuned SGD with momentum on this easy problem, and all the optimisers end within about one standard error (0.9 points on 359 validation images) of each other: on an easy problem the optimiser changes the speed, not the destination.
A constant learning rate ends 17% above the noise floor and jitters from epoch to epoch; both decaying schedules end within 0.5% of the floor (s9: the excess loss is proportional to η).
Adam's first step moves almost every parameter by η whatever the size of its gradient — sign descent, as m̂/√v̂ = g/|g| predicts at t = 1.
extensions: Add RMSprop and Adagrad (torch.optim) to the shoot-out.
Repeat the shoot-out with six hidden layers of 64 units and find where plain SGD stops working.
Run AdamW at η = 3×10⁻² (above the range test's minimum) with and without a 5% warmup, and plot the first 100 steps of each.
Repeat part 4 with three seeds at η = 0.02 and η = 0.05 and average the final MSE of the constant schedule, to separate the trend (excess ∝ η) from the randomness of the last point.

labs.title: Digits, honestly: a complete PyTorch training run
labs.goal: Train an MLP classifier on handwritten digits under a proper train/validation/test protocol: sanity checks before training, early stopping on the validation loss, per-layer monitoring, a single test evaluation with its standard error, and the spread over seeds.
labs.data: load_digits from scikit-learn: 1,797 grey-level 8×8 images with values 0–16 and 10 balanced classes (174–183 images each), shipped with the package.
steps: Load and split 60/20/20 with train_test_split (stratify, random_state = 0) into 1,078/359/360. Compute the per-pixel training mean and standard deviation; print the pixels with zero standard deviation on the training set (indices 0, 24, 32 and 39) and show that naive standardisation produces 1,436 non-finite values in the validation set (4 pixels × 359 images); replace zero standard deviations by 1 and standardise all three splits with the training statistics.

Model 64 → 128 → 128 → 10 with ReLU and a Dropout(p) slot set to p = 0 for now, written as an nn.Module subclass (layers created in __init__, composed in forward; the ReLUs as named submodules so hooks can attach to them) — the form Module 03 builds on. With torch.manual_seed(0) it draws the same initial weights as the nn.Sequential version of Lab 3. Print the parameter count (26,122) and the initial training loss (2.309, against ln 10 = 2.303).
Overfit one batch: 32 training images, AdamW at 10⁻³ without weight decay, 200 steps; print the loss at steps 0, 50, 100 and 200: 2.31, 0.046, 0.0037, 0.0012.

Train: AdamW (η = 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻²), cosine schedule over 100 epochs, batch 64, early stopping on the validation loss with patience 15, keeping the best state_dict (copy.deepcopy). Print the training loss, validation loss and validation accuracy every 10 epochs: epoch 10 — 0.0419, 0.150, 0.964; 20 — 0.0086, 0.121, 0.969; 30 — 0.0037, 0.116, 0.969; 40 — 0.0022, 0.115, 0.964; early stop at epoch 44 with best epoch 29 (validation loss 0.1145). About 1.5 s.

Monitoring with forward hooks on the ReLU modules at epochs 1, 10 and 30 (one full-batch pass in training mode): the activation standard deviation of both hidden layers, the fraction of dead units, the gradient norm of each weight matrix, and the update-to-weight ratio of the last step (copy each weight before opt.step()). Expected roughly: standard deviations 0.37/0.22, 0.62/1.01, 0.68/1.24; dead fractions 0/0.008, 0/0.016, 0/0.016; gradient norms 0.25/0.32/0.39, 0.029/0.020/0.042, 0.004/0.003/0.005; update ratios about 10⁻², 2×10⁻³ and 2.5×10⁻⁴.

Restore the best checkpoint and evaluate once on the test set: accuracy 0.9694 with standard error √(p(1 − p)/360) = 0.0091. Print the confusion matrix and list the 11 misclassified test images as (true, predicted) pairs.
Repeat steps 4 and 6 for seeds 0–4 and print the test accuracies and their mean ± standard deviation: 0.9694, 0.9750, 0.9750, 0.9722, 0.9778 → 97.39% ± 0.32. About 15 s.
expected_observations: Two of the sanity checks catch real problems before any training: constant pixels break naive standardisation, and the initial loss confirms the initialisation.
The training loss keeps falling (to 0.002) after the validation loss has flattened near 0.115: the gap is overfitting, and early stopping picks epoch 29.
Hidden activations stay of order one and dead units below 2%: nothing in the monitoring needs action, which is what a healthy run looks like.
The test standard error (0.9 points) is about three times the seed spread (0.3 points); both bound what any comparison on this data can show.
An MLP sees the 8×8 image as 64 unrelated numbers; Module 03's convolutional networks build in the structure it ignores.
extensions: Set the dropout slots to p = 0.2 and compare the validation loss, the best epoch and the test accuracy over the same five seeds.

Calibration (s11): fit a temperature T on the validation logits by a grid search over [0.05, 5] minimising the NLL, and compare the test NLL and expected calibration error (Module 01) before and after (expected T ≈ 1.20; test NLL 0.134 → 0.124). Then retrain with label smoothing 0.1 and repeat (expected: underconfident, calibration error about 0.12, fitted T ≈ 0.49).
Replace AdamW by SGD with momentum 0.9 at Lab 3's chosen η = 0.05 and compare.
Train on 25%, 50% and 100% of the training split and plot test accuracy against N: 'more data', measured.

labs.title: Debugging clinic: four broken training scripts
labs.goal: Diagnose and fix four training scripts that run without errors but are wrong, using their symptoms and the checklist of s14.
labs.data: load_digits, split and standardised exactly as in Lab 4.
steps: Run the reference script (Lab 4's model, Adam at η = 10⁻³, 20 epochs, no early stopping) and keep its log as the healthy baseline. Every script prints the same fields: the initial loss, the epoch-mean training loss, the validation loss and accuracy (computed correctly by a shared evaluate function), the last global gradient norm and the fraction of dead units in layer 1. Baseline: initial loss 2.309; epoch 1 — training loss 2.08, validation accuracy 0.763; epoch 5 — 0.191, 0.928; epoch 10 — 0.049, 0.964; epoch 20 — 0.009, 0.969; gradient norm falling from 0.69 to 0.064; no dead units.

Script A (the wrong loss input: F.cross_entropy(F.softmax(logits, 1), y)). Symptom to find in its log: training loss 2.27, 1.61, 1.49, 1.469 at epochs 1, 5, 10 and 20 — a plateau just above 1.461 = −ln(e/(e + 9)) — while the validation accuracy rises to 0.967 and the gradient norm is 2–5 times smaller than the baseline's (0.13 against 0.69 at epoch 1, 0.031 against 0.064 at epoch 20). Diagnosis: probabilities fed in as logits (s12). Fix: pass the logits.

Script B (missing opt.zero_grad()). Symptom: the gradient norm grows every epoch (7.0, 23, 146, 194) while the training loss falls to 0.33 at epoch 5, then climbs to 1.8 and wanders; validation accuracy peaks near 0.88 and decays to 0.80. Diagnosis: .grad accumulates across steps, so every update uses the sum of all past gradients (s4). Fix: zero the gradients every step.

Script C (a bad initialisation: every nn.Linear weight drawn from 𝒩(0, 1) with nn.init.normal_). Symptom: an initial loss of 677 instead of about 2.3; training loss 576, 136, 43, 8.6 at epochs 1, 5, 10, 20; validation loss 44 and accuracy 0.80 at epoch 20. Diagnosis: logits hundreds of units large, so the softmax is saturated and confidently wrong; s14's initial-loss check catches it before training. Fix: remove the custom initialisation (PyTorch's default) or use He initialisation.

Script D (an evaluation-mode mistake: a model with BatchNorm1d and Dropout(0.5), evaluated without model.eval()). Symptom: two consecutive evaluations of the same weights give different accuracies (0.922 and 0.930 at epoch 20), evaluating in batches of 8 gives 0.844, and the same weights in evaluation mode give 0.967. Diagnosis: dropout masks and batch statistics are active during evaluation (s10, s11). Fix: model.eval() and torch.no_grad() for evaluation, model.train() before the next epoch.

For each script write the diagnosis as one line 'symptom → cause → fix', apply the fix, rerun, and confirm that the log now has the baseline's shape. Finally run s14's checklist on script C before training, to show that its step 4 (the initial loss) would have stopped the run at step 0.
expected_observations: None of the four scripts raises an error; each has a numeric signature — a floor at 1.46, a growing gradient norm, an absurd initial loss, evaluations that do not repeat — that is readable within the first minute.
Accuracy alone can hide a bug: script A reaches 96.7% validation accuracy while its training loss is meaningless.
Logging the initial loss and the gradient norm costs a line each and diagnoses two of the four bugs.
extensions: Script E: Adam at η = 0.1. Expected symptom: the training loss rises above its initial value (3.15 at epoch 1) and validation accuracy falls from 0.74 to 0.29 by epoch 20. Diagnose it with Lab 3's range test.

Script F: a regression version (Lab 1's y = sin 3x in PyTorch) with targets of shape (B,) and predictions of shape (B, 1): find PyTorch's broadcasting warning and the loss stuck at the variance of the targets (0.517 with torch.manual_seed(0) and 256 points; s2).

Script G: standardisation statistics computed on all 1,797 images; measure how much the test accuracy changes, and explain why leakage of this kind is small here and can be large elsewhere (Module 01).

exercises.prompt: A colleague trains a network with three hidden layers of 64 units but forgot the activation functions. (a) Show that the network computes an affine function of its input, and write its effective weight matrix and bias in terms of W⁽¹⁾…W⁽⁴⁾ and b⁽¹⁾…b⁽⁴⁾ (this module's convention, z = W⊤h + b). (b) The colleague then adds a ReLU after the third hidden layer only. For a two-dimensional input such as the circles data, which functions can the network now represent? Compare it with a network that has a single hidden layer of 64 ReLU units.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) z⁽⁴⁾ = W⁽⁴⁾⊤(W⁽³⁾⊤(W⁽²⁾⊤(W⁽¹⁾⊤x + b⁽¹⁾) + b⁽²⁾) + b⁽³⁾) + b⁽⁴⁾ = W_eff⊤x + b_eff with W_eff = W⁽¹⁾W⁽²⁾W⁽³⁾W⁽⁴⁾ and b_eff = W⁽⁴⁾⊤W⁽³⁾⊤W⁽²⁾⊤b⁽¹⁾ + W⁽⁴⁾⊤W⁽³⁾⊤b⁽²⁾ + W⁽⁴⁾⊤b⁽³⁾ + b⁽⁴⁾. (b) The first three layers still collapse to one affine map, z⁽³⁾ = A⊤x + c with A = W⁽¹⁾W⁽²⁾W⁽³⁾ ∈ ℝ^(2×64) and c = W⁽³⁾⊤W⁽²⁾⊤b⁽¹⁾ + W⁽³⁾⊤b⁽²⁾ + b⁽³⁾, and the ReLU and the output layer follow: a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with 64 units and first-layer weights A. Conversely, any such network is obtained with W⁽¹⁾ = A, W⁽²⁾ = W⁽³⁾ = I, b⁽¹⁾ = b⁽²⁾ = 0 and b⁽³⁾ = c. The two families are identical: sums of 64 ridge functions, whose decision boundaries are polygons that can enclose the disc (s1). The two extra 64 × 64 layers add parameters but no expressiveness; they change only how gradient descent moves through the parameters.

exercises.prompt: A network has three layers: z⁽¹⁾ = W⁽¹⁾⊤x + b⁽¹⁾, h⁽¹⁾ = tanh z⁽¹⁾; z⁽²⁾ = W⁽²⁾⊤h⁽¹⁾ + b⁽²⁾, h⁽²⁾ = tanh z⁽²⁾; z⁽³⁾ = W⁽³⁾⊤h⁽²⁾ + b⁽³⁾, with softmax cross-entropy on z⁽³⁾. (a) Write δ⁽³⁾, δ⁽²⁾, δ⁽¹⁾ and all six parameter gradients for one example. (b) Give their batch-matrix forms for a loss averaged over B examples. (c) Count the FLOPs of the matrix products in the forward and backward passes for widths d₀, d₁, d₂, d₃, and show that backward is at most twice forward. (d) Evaluate the ratio for (784, 256, 256, 10).
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) δ⁽³⁾ = p̂ − y; δ⁽²⁾ = (W⁽³⁾δ⁽³⁾) ⊙ (1 − (h⁽²⁾)²); δ⁽¹⁾ = (W⁽²⁾δ⁽²⁾) ⊙ (1 − (h⁽¹⁾)²); ∂𝓛/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾δ⁽ˡ⁾⊤ with h⁽⁰⁾ = x; ∂𝓛/∂b⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾. (b) Δ⁽³⁾ = (P̂ − Y)/B; Δ⁽²⁾ = (Δ⁽³⁾W⁽³⁾⊤) ⊙ (1 − H⁽²⁾²); Δ⁽¹⁾ = (Δ⁽²⁾W⁽²⁾⊤) ⊙ (1 − H⁽¹⁾²); ∂𝓛/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾⊤Δ⁽ˡ⁾; ∂𝓛/∂b⁽ˡ⁾ = 1⊤Δ⁽ˡ⁾. (c) Forward 2B(d₀d₁ + d₁d₂ + d₂d₃). Backward: weight gradients 2B(d₀d₁ + d₁d₂ + d₂d₃) plus errors passed down 2B(d₁d₂ + d₂d₃) (∂𝓛/∂x is not needed), so the ratio is 1 + (d₁d₂ + d₂d₃)/(d₀d₁ + d₁d₂ + d₂d₃) ≤ 2, with equality only if the input gradient is also computed. (d) d₀d₁ = 200,704, d₁d₂ = 65,536, d₂d₃ = 2,560: ratio 1 + 68,096/268,800 = 1.25. 'Backward ≈ 2 × forward' is an upper bound, approached when the first layer is a small share of the work (the digits network of s3 gives 1.68).

exercises.prompt: s1 compares the sawtooth t^k, the tent map t(x) = 2ReLU(x) − 4ReLU(x − ½) composed with itself k times, with a one-hidden-layer ReLU network that represents the same function. (a) Explain, without counting, why one more composition doubles the number of linear pieces while adding only two units, whereas a one-hidden-layer network must add a unit for every new piece. (b) A colleague concludes that deep networks are always exponentially more efficient than wide ones. Say what the argument establishes, and name two things it does not.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Each linear piece of t^(k−1) maps its interval monotonically onto all of [0, 1]. The tent map rises on [0, ½] and falls on [½, 1], so applying it once more folds every such piece into two, one rising and one falling: the same two units act on every existing piece at once. A one-hidden-layer network on a scalar input can change slope only at its units' breakpoints, x = −b_j/w_j, one per unit, so every new piece costs a new unit. (b) It establishes a separation for a particular family: functions with exponentially many linear pieces that depth represents with exponentially fewer units and parameters (more generally, the number of linear regions can grow exponentially with depth, Montúfar et al. 2014). It does not show that the functions met in practice are of this kind, and it does not show that gradient descent from a random start finds the deep construction; nor does it say anything about generalising from finite data. Depth also brings vanishing gradients (s3), which s5, s6 and s10 address.

exercises.prompt: For f(x₁, x₂) = x₁²x₂ + exp(x₁x₂) at (x₁, x₂) = (1, 2): (a) write the computational graph with named intermediate variables; (b) compute ∂f/∂x₁ in one forward-mode pass with tangent (1, 0); (c) compute both partial derivatives in one reverse-mode pass; (d) for a function ℝⁿ → ℝ, how many passes does each mode need for the full gradient?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) v₁ = x₁² = 1; v₂ = v₁x₂ = 2; v₃ = x₁x₂ = 2; v₄ = exp v₃ = 7.3891; f = v₂ + v₄ = 9.3891. (b) v̇₁ = 2x₁ = 2; v̇₂ = v̇₁x₂ + v₁·0 = 4; v̇₃ = 1·x₂ + x₁·0 = 2; v̇₄ = e²·2 = 14.778; ḟ = 18.778. (c) f̄ = 1; v̄₂ = 1; v̄₄ = 1; v̄₃ = e² = 7.389; v̄₁ = v̄₂x₂ = 2; x̄₁ = v̄₁·2x₁ + v̄₃x₂ = 4 + 14.778 = 18.778; x̄₂ = v̄₂v₁ + v̄₃x₁ = 1 + 7.389 = 8.389. (d) Forward mode n passes; reverse mode one.

exercises.prompt: (a) Using δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ φ'(z⁽ˡ⁾), show that a ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for every training example receives zero gradient on its incoming weights and bias, so plain gradient descent can never revive it; then show that decoupled weight decay cannot revive it either. (b) In Lab 1's code, set b1[5] = −10 after initialisation, train for 3,000 steps, and confirm that the gradients of W1[:, 5] and b1[5] are exactly 0 throughout and that the unit's weight ends where it started. (c) Name two changes that prevent such units or let them recover.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) z_j < 0 for every example gives φ'(z_j) = 0, so δ_j = 0 for every example, hence ∂𝓛/∂W_{:,j} = Σ h δ_j = 0 and ∂𝓛/∂b_j = 0: the parameters never change. Decoupled decay multiplies w_j and b_j by (1 − ηλ), which multiplies every z_j by the same positive factor, so its sign never changes. (b) Lab 1's input lies in [−1, 1] and W1[0, 5] = 0.109 with this seed, so z = 0.109x − 10 < 0 everywhere: the largest gradient seen is exactly 0, W1[0, 5] stays 0.10894, and the other 63 units still reach a training MSE of 2.8×10⁻⁴. (c) A lower learning rate (large updates are what push biases far negative); He initialisation with zero biases; leaky ReLU or GELU, whose derivative is non-zero for z < 0; re-initialising units that monitoring finds dead.

exercises.prompt: A deep stack of square ReLU layers (n_in = n_out = n, no normalisation) is initialised in three ways: He normal (σ_w² = 2/n_in), Glorot normal (σ_w² = 2/(n_in + n_out)) and PyTorch's nn.Linear default (weights and biases from U(−1/√n_in, 1/√n_in)). Without computing: (a) which of the three keeps the scale of the pre-activations constant through depth, and what happens under the other two? (b) Under the default, the measured standard deviation eventually stops falling and settles at a floor. Why, and why does the floor not rescue training? (c) Why do Labs 3–5 get away with the default, and when would you call nn.init.kaiming_normal_ explicitly?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) He: a ReLU halves the second moment and the factor 2 restores it, so the scale is the same at every layer. Glorot reduces to 1/n when n_in = n_out, the tanh-style scale, so the second moment halves at every ReLU layer (the standard deviation falls by √2 per layer). The default's weight variance is 1/(3n), a sixth of He's, so the second moment falls about sixfold per layer. (b) Every layer adds its bias, and the spread of the biases does not shrink with depth; once the propagated signal is smaller than that spread, the biases set the measured scale (s6's floor). But a bias is the same for every input: the part of each activation that depends on x keeps shrinking, so deep layers output nearly the same vector for every input and the early layers receive tiny gradients. (c) Their network has only three weight layers, so the shrinkage compounds over a few layers only and stays tolerable; normalisation layers would also reset the scale at every layer. For a deep ReLU stack without normalisation, such as s6's ten-layer example, use He initialisation explicitly.

exercises.prompt: For 𝓛(θ) = ½(θ₁² + 64θ₂²): (a) the largest stable learning rate for gradient descent; (b) the largest stable η for heavy-ball momentum with μ = 0.9, and for Nesterov momentum with μ = 0.9; (c) the per-step contraction of θ₁ under gradient descent at η = 0.03, and the number of steps to shrink θ₁ by a factor of 1,000; (d) the optimal heavy-ball η and μ and the asymptotic contraction per step.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) η < 2/λ_max = 2/64 = 0.03125. (b) Heavy ball: η < 2(1 + μ)/λ_max = 3.8/64 = 0.0594; Nesterov: η < 2(1 + μ)/((1 + 2μ)λ_max) = 3.8/(2.8·64) = 0.0212, below even gradient descent's limit. (c) 1 − 0.03·1 = 0.97 per step; ln 1,000/(−ln 0.97) = 226.8, so 227 steps (θ₂ is multiplied by 1 − 0.03·64 = −0.92 per step: it oscillates and shrinks by 1,000 in about 83 steps). (d) η = 4/(√64 + √1)² = 4/81 = 0.0494; μ = ((8 − 1)/(8 + 1))² = (7/9)² = 0.605; contraction 7/9 = 0.778 per step, about 28 steps per factor 1,000 asymptotically against 227 for gradient descent: the √κ speed-up. A simulation from (1, 1) needs 44 steps to shrink ‖θ‖ by 1,000, because the double root adds a transient t·0.778^t.

exercises.prompt: Run Adam by hand for two steps on one parameter with gradients g₁ = 1 and g₂ = 3, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε negligible, learning rate η. (a) Give m_t, v_t, m̂_t, v̂_t and the step for t = 1 and t = 2. (b) What would the steps be without bias correction? (c) Prove that for gradients with a constant mean, E[m_t] = (1 − β₁^t)E[g].

In three or four sentences: why is L2 regularisation added to the gradient (torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=λ)) not the same as AdamW's decoupled weight decay? Which parameters does the coupled version regularise least? Which PyTorch call gives the decoupled version, and why does the distinction vanish for plain SGD?
exercises.solution_sketch: Under Adam the L2 term λθ becomes part of g and is divided by √v̂ with the rest of it, so parameter i is shrunk by about ηλθ_i/√v̂_i per step: parameters with large gradient histories are regularised least (gradient RMS 10 against 0.1 gives 10⁻⁸ against 10⁻⁶ per step at η = 10⁻³, λ = 10⁻⁴). AdamW subtracts ηλθ outside the normalisation, the same relative shrinkage for every parameter. torch.optim.AdamW (or Adam with decoupled_weight_decay=True in recent versions). For SGD there is no normalisation, so θ ← θ − η(g + λθ) is exactly decay by (1 − ηλ).

exercises.prompt: Inverted dropout with drop probability p = 0.4: (a) by what factor are surviving activations scaled during training? (b) Show that the expected value of a unit's output is unchanged. (c) What goes wrong at evaluation if model.eval() is forgotten? (d) What would go wrong if the scaling were omitted during training while dropout is still switched off at evaluation?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) 1/(1 − 0.4) = 5/3 ≈ 1.67. (b) E[h̃] = 0.6·(5/3)h + 0.4·0 = h. (c) Random masks at evaluation: predictions change from call to call and accuracy drops (Lab 5, script D: 92–93% against 96.7%). (d) During training the next layer sees inputs with expectation 0.6h, at evaluation h: inputs 1.67 times larger than anything it was trained on, a systematic shift.

exercises.prompt: (a) Derive log Σ_j e^(z_j) = m + log Σ_j e^(z_j − m) for any m, and explain why m = max_j z_j makes the right-hand side safe from both overflow and log 0. (b) Compute by hand the cross-entropy for logits z = (800, 803, 799) with target class 0. (c) In NumPy, show that the naive −log(softmax(z)[0]) returns nan in float64 for these logits, and find the smallest integer logit at which np.exp overflows in float64.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Σ e^(z_j) = e^m Σ e^(z_j − m); take logarithms. With m = max, every exponent is ≤ 0, so no term exceeds 1 (no overflow), and one term equals 1, so the sum is ≥ 1 and its log ≥ 0 (no log 0). (b) m = 803; Σ e^(z − m) = e⁻³ + 1 + e⁻⁴ = 0.049787 + 1 + 0.018316 = 1.068103; logsumexp = 803 + ln 1.068103 = 803.065884; loss = 803.065884 − 800 = 3.065884 (F.cross_entropy gives 3.0659). The target is not the largest logit, so the loss is the 3-unit gap plus a small correction. (c) np.exp(800) = inf, with an overflow warning, and inf/inf = nan. float64's largest value is 1.80×10³⁰⁸ = e^709.78: np.exp(709.0) = 8.2×10³⁰⁷ and np.exp(710.0) = inf, so 710.

exercises.prompt: A 10-class network ends in a softmax layer, and its outputs are passed to F.cross_entropy, which applies log-softmax again. Without computing the bound: (a) why can the training loss not approach zero, and why is its floor higher for more classes? (b) Why does the accuracy still improve during training? (c) Why are the gradients that reach the network small, and why do they shrink further as the network becomes confident?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) The second softmax receives 'logits' that are probabilities: each in [0, 1], summing to 1. The largest lead the true class can have over the others is 1, so the probability it is given is at most e/(e + K − 1), bounded away from 1, and the loss −ln p̂_y is bounded away from 0 (s12 evaluates the floor). With more classes, more competitors share the remaining mass, so the bound falls and the floor rises. (b) The softmax preserves order: the class with the largest probability is the class with the largest real logit, so the network can still learn the ranking, and accuracy counts only the ranking. (c) The gradient with respect to the real logits passes through the extra softmax's Jacobian, diag(p̂) − p̂p̂⊤ (s3), whose entries are at most 1/4 in size and all tend to 0 as p̂ approaches a one-hot vector, while the loss's own gradient stays bounded away from zero because of the floor. The more confident the network, the less gradient it receives, and the loss stalls (Lab 5's script A: gradient norms 2–5 times below the baseline's). The fix is to pass the logits.

exercises.prompt: Three gradient checks of hand-written backward passes, each using central differences and the per-entry relative error |a − n|/max(10⁻⁸, |a| + |n|). For each, say whether it points to a bug and what you would do next. (a) A float64 check at ε = 10⁻¹¹ reports errors between 10⁻⁷ and 10⁻⁴, scattered over every tensor with no pattern. (b) A float64 check at ε = 10⁻⁵ reports errors below 10⁻⁹ everywhere except one entry of the first layer's bias, in a ReLU layer, at 3×10⁻³; that entry's error changes erratically as ε is varied. (c) A float64 check at ε = 10⁻⁵ reports errors between 0.2 and 1 for every entry of the first layer's weights and bias, and below 10⁻⁸ for the second layer's.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Probably not a bug: ε is far too small, so the rounding error of the difference quotient, which grows as ε shrinks, swamps the truncation error; the errors are spread over every tensor rather than concentrated in one. Rerun at ε ≈ 10⁻⁵ (s14); a real bug survives the change. (b) Probably not a bug: a single entry in a ReLU layer that is sensitive to ε is the signature of a kink. Some example's pre-activation for that unit lies within ε of zero, so the two evaluations straddle it and the quotient averages two slopes. Print the smallest |z| of that unit over the batch (Lab 1 found 2×10⁻⁷); a smaller ε, or a slightly perturbed point, makes the entry agree. (c) A bug, and the check localises it: the second layer's gradients are right and everything below them is wrong, so the error is in the step that passes δ from the second layer to the first — a missing or wrong ReLU gate, or a wrong transpose. Lab 1's step 4 produces exactly this pattern by dropping the gate.

exercises.prompt: Name the most likely cause and the first thing to try for each run of a 10-class classifier: (a) the loss starts at 2.30 and stays there; (b) the loss falls from 2.3 to 0.4 over the first 200 steps, then jumps to 9 at step 230 and becomes NaN at step 240, the gradient norm spiking just before; (c) the training loss is 0.02 and falling while the validation loss is 0.9 and has risen since epoch 8; (d) training and validation losses both stall at 0.9 from epoch 5, where a step schedule cut the learning rate by a factor of 100.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) No learning signal (dead units, a detached graph, a zero learning rate, labels misaligned with inputs): overfit one batch and print per-layer gradient norms. (b) A learning rate too high for this stage of training (s14's 'falls, then spikes'), possibly tipped over by a bad batch or an overflow: lower η (a range test, s9), add warmup if there is none, clip the global gradient norm at 1.0 and compute the loss from logits; torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) names the first non-finite operation if that is not enough. The gradient norm spiking before the loss is the tell (Figure 2.21 (b)); had it grown steadily from the start, a missing zero_grad would be the suspect. (c) Overfitting: early stopping at about epoch 8, weight decay, augmentation, more data. (d) The learning rate decayed too early: a longer schedule or cosine decay; then check whether the model is too small (underfitting).

exercises.prompt: In Lab 1's NumPy network, implement Adam with bias correction as a drop-in replacement for the update line. (a) For SGD and for Adam, find the best learning rate on a grid of factors of about 3 over 3,000 full-batch steps, and compare the final training MSE and the loss curves. (b) Multiply X by 1,000, as if the input had been recorded in millimetres instead of metres, and repeat without re-standardising. (c) Explain what changed for each optimiser, and what fixes both.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) SGD's best is η ≈ 0.1 with MSE 1.1×10⁻⁴ (0.3 is unstable); Adam's best is η ≈ 3×10⁻³ with MSE 1.4×10⁻⁶, about 80 times lower. (b) With X × 1,000, SGD diverges (NaN) for every η ≥ 10⁻⁶ and is stuck at MSE 0.166 for η ≤ 10⁻⁷: W1's curvature grew by 10⁶ while b1's did not, so no single η suits both. Adam never diverges, because it normalises the gradient's scale, but its best is MSE 0.080 at η = 0.1. (c) Adam's step is about η in parameter units, and the millimetre problem needs W1 near 10⁻³ while b1 stays near 1: Adam fixes a gradient-scale problem but not a parameter-scale one. Standardising the input with its training mean and standard deviation restores the original behaviour for both. (About 20 s for the whole grid on a laptop CPU.)

quiz.question: What does the universal approximation theorem guarantee for a network with one hidden layer and a non-polynomial activation?
options: For any continuous function on a compact set and any ε > 0, some finite width achieves error below ε everywhere on that set.
Gradient descent from a random initialisation reaches any target error if the layer is wide enough.
The width needed grows at most linearly with the input dimension.
A network that fits the training data within ε also has error below ε on unseen inputs.
quiz.explanation: The theorem is about existence only. It says nothing about whether training finds the weights (B); constructions can need a number of units exponential in the input dimension (C); and generalisation from finite data is a separate question (D, Module 01).

quiz.question: In a batch of B = 32, layer l has input H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ ∈ ℝ^(32×100), weights W⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(100×50) and error signals Δ⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(32×50). Which expression is ∂𝓛/∂W⁽ˡ⁾?
options: Δ⁽ˡ⁾⊤H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾, of shape 50 × 100
Δ⁽ˡ⁾W⁽ˡ⁾⊤, of shape 32 × 100
H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾⊤Δ⁽ˡ⁾, of shape 100 × 50
H⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾W⁽ˡ⁾, of shape 32 × 50
quiz.explanation: The gradient has the shape of W (100 × 50) and is the sum over the batch of the outer products hδ⊤, which is H⊤Δ. The first option is its transpose (the layout PyTorch stores, not this module's convention); the second is the error passed to the previous layer before gating by φ'; the last is the forward pre-activation without its bias.

quiz.question: A scalar loss depends on n = 10⁶ parameters. Which statement about computing its gradient is correct?
options: Forward mode needs one pass; reverse mode needs 10⁶.
Reverse mode needs one backward pass costing a small multiple of the forward pass; forward mode would need about 10⁶ passes.
Both modes need 10⁶ passes, but reverse-mode passes are cheaper.
Reverse mode needs one pass and no memory beyond the parameters.
quiz.explanation: Reverse mode computes one row of the Jacobian (a vector-Jacobian product) per pass, and a scalar loss has one row; forward mode computes one column per pass. Reverse mode's price is memory — the forward values must be stored or recomputed — so the last option is wrong.

quiz.question: Which property made ReLU the default hidden activation over the sigmoid in deep networks?
options: It is smooth everywhere, which helps the optimiser.
Its derivative is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so it does not shrink backpropagated errors on the active side.
Its outputs are zero-centred.
It cannot produce units that stop learning.
quiz.explanation: The sigmoid multiplies the error by at most 1/4 per layer. ReLU has a kink at 0 (GELU and SiLU are the smooth ones), its outputs are non-negative rather than zero-centred, and dead units are precisely its failure mode.

quiz.question: Why does He initialisation use Var(w) = 2/n_in for ReLU layers, twice the 1/n_in used for tanh?
options: A ReLU sets negative pre-activations to zero, so E[h²] = Var(z)/2; doubling the weight variance keeps Var(z) the same from layer to layer.
ReLU outputs have twice the variance of their inputs.
To balance the forward and backward passes, as Glorot initialisation does.
Because the ReLU's derivative is 2 on its active side.
quiz.explanation: Var(z_next) = nσ_w²E[h²] and, for a symmetric z, E[ReLU(z)²] = Var(z)/2. The second option is false (the output variance is 0.34 Var(z)); the third describes Glorot's 2/(n_in + n_out); the derivative is 1, not 2.

quiz.question: Heavy-ball momentum with μ = 0.9 receives one gradient component that is constant from step to step and another that flips sign every step. In the steady state the velocity scales them by about:
options: 10 and 10
quiz.explanation: The velocity is the gradient passed through a filter with gain 1/(1 − μ) = 10 at zero frequency and 1/(1 + μ) ≈ 0.53 at the alternating frequency: momentum is a low-pass filter that damps oscillation across a valley and accelerates progress along it.

quiz.question: Adam with β₁ = 0.9 and β₂ = 0.999 takes its first step without bias correction. Compared with the corrected step (about η per coordinate), the uncorrected step is:
options: About 10 times smaller, because m₁ = 0.1g.
About 3.16 times larger, because v₁ = 0.001g² is depleted more than m₁ = 0.1g.
The same, because the two corrections cancel.
About 1,000 times larger, because v₁ = 0.001g².
quiz.explanation: m₁/√v₁ = 0.1g/(0.0316|g|) = 3.16·sign(g). The first option ignores the depletion of v, the last ignores m's and the square root. The ratio (1 − β₁^t)/√(1 − β₂^t) keeps growing to about 6.6 near t = 12 before returning to 1.

quiz.question: Why is L2 regularisation added to the gradient not the same as AdamW's decoupled weight decay when the optimiser is Adam?
options: They are identical up to a rescaling of λ, exactly as for SGD.
AdamW decays only the biases.
L2 regularisation is applied only at evaluation time.
The L2 term is divided by √v̂ like the rest of the gradient, so parameters with large gradient histories are decayed less; AdamW shrinks every parameter by the same factor.
quiz.explanation: For SGD the two coincide, so the first option is true there but not here. Under Adam the coupled penalty is normalised per parameter, and no single L2 coefficient reproduces uniform decay unless v̂ is the same for every parameter.

quiz.question: A network with batch normalisation is evaluated after model.eval(). Which statistics normalise a test input?
options: Running averages of the batch means and variances accumulated during training.
The mean and variance of the current test batch.
The mean and variance across the test input's own features.
None: batch normalisation is switched off in evaluation mode.
quiz.explanation: Evaluation mode replaces batch statistics by running averages, so a prediction does not depend on the batch. The second option is what happens when eval() is forgotten; the third describes layer normalisation; the layer is not switched off — it still normalises and applies γ and β.

quiz.question: Inverted dropout with p = 0.25 is applied to a hidden activation h. What happens during training and at evaluation?
options: Training: zeroed with probability 0.25; evaluation: multiplied by 0.75.
Training: multiplied by 0.75; evaluation: zeroed with probability 0.25.
Training: zeroed with probability 0.25, otherwise multiplied by 4/3; evaluation: unchanged.
Training: zeroed with probability 0.75, otherwise multiplied by 4.
quiz.explanation: Scaling the survivors by 1/(1 − p) = 4/3 keeps E[h̃] = h, so evaluation needs no change. The first option is the original, non-inverted formulation — correct in expectation, but not what frameworks implement; the last confuses p with the keep probability.

quiz.question: Why is bf16 usually preferred to fp16 for training without loss scaling?
options: bf16 has more mantissa bits, so it is more precise.
bf16 represents every integer up to 10⁶ exactly.
fp16 cannot represent negative numbers.
bf16 has fp32's 8 exponent bits, so its range reaches about 3.4×10³⁸, while fp16 overflows above 65,504 and underflows small gradients.
quiz.explanation: bf16 trades precision (7 mantissa bits, machine epsilon 0.0078) for range; fp16 keeps 10 mantissa bits but only 5 exponent bits, which is why fp16 training needs loss scaling.

quiz.question: A new 10-class classifier starts training at a loss of 47 instead of about 2.3. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too small.
The validation set leaked into the training set.
The initial weights are too large, so the logits are large and confidently wrong.
Dropout is active during training.
quiz.explanation: A sensibly initialised network predicts near-uniform probabilities, so its loss is near ln 10 = 2.30 before any step is taken; the learning rate and leakage cannot affect the loss at step 0, and dropout cannot raise it twentyfold. Lab 5's 𝒩(0, 1) initialisation starts at 677.

papers.citation: Rumelhart, D. E., Hinton, G. E., Williams, R. J. "Learning representations by back-propagating errors." Nature 323, 533–536, 1986.
papers.why: The four-page letter that made backpropagation the way networks are trained. It is short, its equations are s3's in other notation, and it already contains momentum, the symmetry-breaking argument for random initialisation, and learned internal features.
papers.read: Read all of it. Skim the paragraph on unrolling a recurrent network near the end, which Module 04 treats properly.
questions: Map the paper's notation to this module's: what are its x_j, y_j, E, ∂E/∂y_j and ∂E/∂x_j, and which of its equations is s3's between-layers equation?
The paper's acceleration method is Δw(t) = −ε∂E/∂w(t) + αΔw(t − 1). Show that it is heavy-ball momentum and relate ε and α to this module's η and μ.
Why do the authors start from small random weights, and which section of this module makes the same argument?
In the family-tree task, what do the hidden units come to encode, and why is that an instance of s1's learned features?
Which error measure and output nonlinearity does the paper use, and what would Module 01 recommend instead for a classification output?

papers.citation: Glorot, X., Bengio, Y. "Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks." AISTATS, 2010.
papers.why: The experimental paper behind Xavier initialisation. It shows layer by layer how activations saturate and gradients shrink in deep sigmoid and tanh networks, and derives the 2/(n_in + n_out) variance used in s6. Read after s10, it also shows the problem that normalisation layers later solved during training as well as at initialisation.
papers.read: Read Section 1, the experiments with sigmoid and tanh units in Section 3, and Section 4 on gradients at initialisation, including the theoretical derivation of the normalised initialisation and the histograms of activations and back-propagated gradients. Skim Section 2 (data sets and set-up) and the softsign experiments; read the conclusions in Section 5.
questions: The derivation assumes units in their linear regime at initialisation. State the forward and backward conditions on Var(W) it obtains, and why both cannot hold unless n_in = n_out.
Show that the uniform range ±√6/√(n_in + n_out) gives Var(W) = 2/(n_in + n_out).
What happens to the top hidden layer of the sigmoid network early in training, and how do the authors explain it? Connect your answer to s5's zero-centring argument.
Which cost function do the authors find trains better, and how does that agree with Module 01's argument about cross-entropy against squared error?
The paper predates the wide use of ReLU. What changes in its derivation for ReLU units (He et al. 2015), and why does batch normalisation (2015) make the exact initial scale matter less?

papers.citation: Loshchilov, I., Hutter, F. "Decoupled weight decay regularization." ICLR, 2019.
papers.why: The paper behind AdamW, which is what 'Adam' means in modern practice. It proves that L2 regularisation and weight decay coincide for SGD but not for adaptive methods, and shows that decoupling makes the best weight decay nearly independent of the learning rate.
papers.read: Read Section 1, Section 2 (the propositions and Algorithm 2, where the decoupled term is highlighted) and the experiment in Section 4 that maps the final test error over the grid of learning rate and weight decay for Adam and AdamW. Skip Section 3 (the Bayesian-filtering justification) and the warm-restart (AdamWR) experiments.
questions: Restate Proposition 1 in this module's notation: which L2 coefficient makes SGD with L2 regularisation identical to SGD with weight decay?
Explain Proposition 2 in one sentence using s8's derivation: why does no L2 coefficient reproduce decoupled weight decay under Adam?
Compare the shape of the good region in the learning-rate × weight-decay heatmaps for Adam and for AdamW. Why does AdamW's shape make hyperparameter search cheaper?
In PyTorch, which of torch.optim.Adam(weight_decay=λ) and torch.optim.AdamW(weight_decay=λ) implements the paper's Algorithm 2 with the decoupled term?

widgets.name: mlp-playground
widgets.teaching_point: A hidden layer learns its own features: each ReLU unit is a half-plane ramp, the output adds them, and the decision boundary becomes whatever polygon those features allow; with no hidden layer, or with identity activations, the boundary stays a straight line.
controls: select: dataset — circles (default), moons, xor, spiral
slider: noise standard deviation 0–0.3, step 0.01 (default 0.05); changing it regenerates the data with the same seed
slider: hidden layers 0–3, integer (default 1)
slider: units per hidden layer 1–32, integer (default 8)
select: activation — ReLU (default), leaky ReLU (a = 0.01), tanh, sigmoid, none (identity)
select: optimiser — gradient descent, gradient descent + momentum 0.9, Adam (β₁ 0.9, β₂ 0.999, ε 10⁻⁸) (default Adam)
slider: learning rate 0.001–10, log scale (default 0.03)
slider: steps per animation frame 1–20, integer (default 1)
number input: seed (default 1), used for the data and the initialisation
buttons: Play/Pause, Step (one step), Reset weights (re-initialise and clear the charts), New data (next seed)
toggle: show test points (default off)
displays: Main canvas (square, 400 px or the container width on a phone): the input region [−1.5, 1.5]² coloured by the predicted probability p̂(x) = σ(z(x)) on an 80 × 80 grid (two class colours, saturation proportional to |p̂ − 0.5|), the decision boundary p̂ = 0.5 drawn as a contour line, training points as filled circles in their class colours, and test points as hollow circles when shown.
Loss chart: training and test binary cross-entropy against step on a log y-axis, showing the last 2,000 steps.

Readouts: step, training loss, test loss, training and test accuracy, number of parameters, and number of dead units in the first hidden layer (ReLU only: units whose output is 0 for every training point).

Feature thumbnails: for each unit of the first hidden layer (up to 32), a 48 × 48 map of its activation h_j(x) over the input region in a sequential palette, with dead units outlined in grey; with two or more hidden layers, a second row for the second hidden layer (features of features).
widgets.defaults: Circles, noise 0.05, one hidden layer of 8 ReLU units, Adam at η = 0.03, one step per frame, seed 1, paused and showing the random initial boundary. Pressing Play closes the boundary around the inner disc within about a second (about 60 steps at 60 frames per second) and drives the training loss below 0.01 within about ten seconds, while the thumbnails show eight half-plane ramps whose sum makes the polygon. The caption suggests three experiments: set hidden layers to 0 (accuracy stays near 50%); choose the activation 'none' with three hidden layers (the same straight line); set the units to 2 and then 3 (a wedge cannot enclose the disc; a triangle can).
widgets.spec: Data: a seeded generator (mulberry32 of the seed; normal deviates by Box–Muller) makes 100 training points per class and, with seed + 1000, 100 test points per class. circles: class 0 radius U(0, 0.45), class 1 radius U(0.65, 0.95), angle U(0, 2π). moons: class 0 at (cos t, sin t) and class 1 at (1 − cos t, 0.5 − sin t) with t ~ U(0, π), then shifted by (−0.5, −0.25) and scaled by 0.8. xor: centres (±0.5, ±0.5), class 1 where the two signs agree, each point spread by 𝒩(0, 0.15²) per coordinate. spiral: for i = 0 … 99, r = 0.05 + 0.9·i/100 and θ = 3.5π·i/100 + cπ for class c, point (r sin θ, r cos θ). Every point then gets 𝒩(0, noise²) per coordinate. Labels y ∈ {0, 1}. Network: layer sizes [2, H, …, H, 1] with 0–3 hidden layers; z = W⊤h + b per layer; the selected hidden activation; a single output logit. Initialisation: hidden layers He normal (standard deviation √(2/fan_in)) for ReLU and leaky ReLU, Glorot normal (√(2/(fan_in + fan_out))) for tanh, sigmoid and none; output layer Glorot normal; biases zero. Loss: the mean over training points of the stable binary cross-entropy max(z, 0) − zy + log(1 + e^(−|z|)); its gradient with respect to z is (σ(z) − y)/N. Backpropagation exactly as in s3, with φ' = 𝟙[z > 0], a or 1, 1 − h², h(1 − h), or 1. Full-batch updates: GD θ ← θ − ηg; momentum v ← 0.9v + g, θ ← θ − ηv; Adam with bias correction as in s8. Changing the dataset, noise, number of layers, units, activation or seed re-initialises the weights and clears the charts; changing the learning rate does not; changing the optimiser keeps the weights and resets the optimiser's state. After every step, if the loss is not finite or exceeds 10⁶, pause and show 'Diverged — lower the learning rate and press Reset'. Redraw the grid, thumbnails and charts once per animation frame, not once per step. Use Float64Array throughout; a step costs about 200 × (number of weights) multiply-adds, well under a millisecond for the largest setting (3 × 32 units, 2,241 parameters). Pause the animation when the widget is scrolled out of view. Works at 400 px width (controls stack under the canvas) and in light and dark themes. Reference behaviour from a NumPy simulation of this specification (expect small differences from the different random generator): the defaults reach 100% training accuracy at about step 58 and loss 0.005 by step 600; 0 hidden layers, or 'none' with any depth, stay at 53.5% with loss ln 2; 2 units reach 84.5%, 3 units 100% by about step 245; Adam at η = 1 leaves about half the ReLU units dead; GD at η = 10 kills all of them (loss stuck near 1.04, 50%); sigmoid with GD at η = 0.3 is still at chance after 600 steps; on the spiral, 2 × 16 ReLU reaches 100% training accuracy at about step 740, 1 × 64 at about step 2,430, and 1 × 16 reaches only 74% in 3,000 steps.

widgets.name: optimiser-paths
widgets.teaching_point: On an ill-conditioned valley, gradient descent must take steps small enough for the steep direction and so crawls along the shallow one; momentum averages the gradient so the oscillation cancels and the consistent component accumulates; Adam rescales each coordinate, which helps only when the valley is aligned with the axes.
controls: select: surface — ravine (quadratic) (default), banana ((1 − x)² + 10(y − x²)²)
slider: condition number κ of the ravine 1–100, log scale (default 50)
slider: rotation α of the ravine 0–90° (default 0)
checkboxes: methods shown — gradient descent (on), heavy ball (on), Nesterov (off), RMSProp (off), Adam (on)
slider: η for GD, heavy ball and Nesterov, 0.001–0.2, log scale (default 0.035)
slider: momentum μ 0–0.99 (default 0.9)
slider: η for RMSProp and Adam, 0.001–0.5, log scale (default 0.05)
slider: gradient noise σ 0–1 (default 0)
select: schedule — constant (default), cosine to 0 over 300 steps
buttons: Play/Pause, Step, Reset; clicking or tapping the contour plot moves the start point
displays: Contour plot of the surface over [−2, 2]² (ravine) or [−2, 2] × [−1, 3] (banana) with log-spaced contour levels, the minimum marked, and each method's path as a coloured polyline with a dot per step and a larger dot at the current point.
Loss against step for every method shown, on a log y-axis down to 10⁻¹², with a horizontal line at 10⁻⁶ × the initial loss.
Readouts per method: the current loss, the step at which the loss first fell below 10⁻⁶ × L₀ (or '—'), and 'diverged at step t' when it did.

A stability panel for the ravine: λ_max = κ and the limits η < 2/κ (GD), η < 2(1 + μ)/κ (heavy ball) and η < 2(1 + μ)/((1 + 2μ)κ) (Nesterov), each shown in green if the current η is inside it and in red if not.
widgets.defaults: Ravine with κ = 50 and α = 0°, start at (u, v) = (−1.8, 0.35) in the ravine's own coordinates (L₀ = 4.68); GD, heavy ball and Adam shown; η = 0.035, μ = 0.9, adaptive η = 0.05; no noise; constant schedule; paused at step 0. Playing for 300 steps shows GD zig-zagging across the valley (each step multiplies the steep coordinate by −0.75) and reaching 10⁻⁶L₀ at about step 179, heavy ball arriving along a smooth, overshooting path at about step 110, and Adam at about step 126. Setting α = 45° leaves GD and heavy ball exactly as before and slows Adam to about step 214; ticking Nesterov at the default η shows it diverge (0.035 is above its limit of 0.027), while at η = 0.025 it arrives first, at about step 55.
widgets.spec: Ravine: 𝓛(θ) = ½(u² + κv²) with u = cos α·θ₁ + sin α·θ₂ and v = −sin α·θ₁ + cos α·θ₂, gradient Rᵀdiag(1, κ)Rθ where R is that rotation. The start point is stored in (u, v) and mapped to θ = Rᵀ(u, v), so rotating the ravine carries the start point with it and L₀ does not change. Banana: 𝓛 = (1 − x)² + 10(y − x²)², gradient (−2(1 − x) − 40x(y − x²), 20(y − x²)), minimum at (1, 1), default start (−1.5, 1.5) with L₀ = 11.875. Updates, where g is the true gradient plus σξ with ξ ~ 𝒩(0, I) from one seeded generator shared by all methods so that every method sees the same noise sequence: GD θ ← θ − ηg; heavy ball v ← μv + g, θ ← θ − ηv; Nesterov evaluates g at θ − ημv, then v ← μv + g, θ ← θ − ηv; RMSProp s ← 0.9s + 0.1g², θ ← θ − η_a·g/(√s + 10⁻⁸); Adam with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 10⁻⁸ and bias correction, step η_a. The cosine schedule multiplies both learning rates by ½(1 + cos(πt/300)). A method whose loss exceeds 10⁶ or becomes non-finite stops and is labelled 'diverged at step t'. Animate two steps per frame up to 300 steps (1,000 for the banana), then stop. Changing any slider resets every path to the start point; clicking the plot sets a new start point. Works at 400 px width and in light and dark themes. Reference behaviour from a NumPy simulation of this specification: the defaults reach 10⁻⁶L₀ at steps 179 (GD), 110 (heavy ball) and 126 (Adam); at α = 15°, 30° and 45° Adam needs about 124, 192 and 214 steps, while GD and heavy ball are unchanged; RMSProp (η_a = 0.05) touches the threshold at step 57 when α = 0 and then hovers near a loss of 0.02, and never reaches it once rotated; Nesterov diverges for η above 0.0271 and needs 55 steps at η = 0.025; on the banana from (−1.5, 1.5), GD at η = 0.02 needs 610 steps, heavy ball (η = 0.01, μ = 0.9) 128, Nesterov (η = 0.01) 31 and Adam (η_a = 0.05) 581; with noise σ = 0.5, heavy ball at η = 0.03 hovers at a mean loss near 0.047 and at η = 0.01 near 0.016, the noise floor ∝ η of s9.

writer_notes: CONVENTIONS. (1) Weights: W⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(d_{l−1} × d_l) everywhere, the source's batch convention. Batch form Z = HW + 1b⊤; one example as a column, z = W⊤h + b. The source's §1 equation φ(W⁽ˡ⁾h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾) used the opposite layout and is corrected to W⁽ˡ⁾⊤h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾; its backprop equations (δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ φ', ∂𝓛/∂W = hδ⊤) and its NumPy code already use this convention. Say once, in s2, that PyTorch's nn.Linear stores (d_out, d_in). (2) Symbols: δ⁽ˡ⁾ = ∂𝓛/∂z⁽ˡ⁾ for one example and Δ⁽ˡ⁾ ∈ ℝ^(B × d_l) for a batch; φ is the generic activation and σ(·) with an argument is always the sigmoid (write σ_w, σ_B, σ² with subscripts for spreads); calligraphic 𝓛 is the loss, italic L the depth; K classes; B batch size; η learning rate; μ heavy-ball momentum; β₁, β₂ Adam; ε for Adam and normalisation constants, and ε_fd in s14 for the finite-difference step (code may keep eps); p is the dropout probability and p̂ the predicted probabilities; α is the label-smoothing weight; a = 0.01 the leaky-ReLU slope; κ the condition number; λ_i (with subscript) Hessian eigenvalues and λ (no subscript) the weight-decay coefficient, never in the same equation; m in s10 is batch norm's running-average weight. Natural logarithms. Render the maths in LaTeX in the final pages; the outline uses Unicode for readability. (3) PyTorch's weight_decay = λ corresponds to the penalty (λ/2)‖θ‖²; Module 01 writes λ‖θ‖². State the factor of 2 once (s8). RUNNING EXAMPLES, keep the numbers consistent across parts: the tiny 2-2-1 ReLU network with x = (2, 1) (s2 forward, s3 backward and finite-difference check, s4 as VJP rules); sin 3x on [−1, 1] (s1 interpolation, Lab 1, e15); the digits network 64 → 128 → 128 → 10 with 26,122 parameters on the 1,078/359/360 split (s2 counts, s3 cost, s8 Adam's first step, s11, s14, Labs 3–5); the quadratic ½(θ₁² + 100θ₂²) (s7; e7 uses ½(θ₁² + 64θ₂²) so that the exercise does not repeat the worked example); the κ = 50 ravine (optimiser-paths widget); the circles problem (playground, s13). PROVENANCE OF NUMBERS: every number in this outline was computed on 1 October 2026 in the lab environment (Python 3.11.8, NumPy 2.4.6, PyTorch 2.14.1 CPU build, scikit-learn 1.9.1, 4 threads). Lab outputs will be regenerated when the labs are executed; when they are, update the same numbers wherever s1–s14, the What goes wrong list, the exercises and the quiz quote them (search for 2.309, 677, 1.469, 0.0122, 97.39, 0.055, 2.3×10⁻³, 786, 66,440). The widget numbers come from NumPy simulations of the widget specifications; the JavaScript widgets use a different random generator, so quote them as 'about' and describe behaviour qualitatively. CORRECTIONS TO THE SOURCE (make them silently, in the new text): the NumPy example's comment '~1e-3' — the measured final training MSE is 2.8×10⁻⁴; Var(z) = nσ_w²σ_h² holds only for zero-mean h — use the second moment E[h²]; 'a ReLU halves the variance' — it halves the second moment (the variance becomes 0.34 Var(z)); 'backward is about twice forward' — at most twice (1.68 for the digits network, 1.25 for 784-256-256-10), because the first layer's input gradient is never computed; the §10 loop prints the last mini-batch's loss, not the epoch's. DEPARTURES FROM THE EDITOR'S SUGGESTIONS: (a) the labs follow the reading order, so the optimiser shoot-out is Lab 3 and the digits protocol is Lab 4 (the suggestion had them the other way round); Lab 4 reuses Lab 3's data and model, but each lab still loads them itself so that it runs on its own. (b) The source's Exercise 2 (He against 𝒩(0, 1) and 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴)) became Lab 1's step 7, run over ten seeds, because on this shallow network a single seed is misleading: with the source's own seed order the 𝒩(0, 1) run starts at a loss of only 0.58, and the initial loss ranges from 0.32 to 24 across seeds. (c) A second widget, optimiser-paths, was added for s7–s8, because the geometry of momentum and the rotation-dependence of Adam are the hardest things to get from text. (d) The complete training loop has its own short section, s13, before the debugging section. (e) AdaGrad and RMSProp are included as the steps from SGD to Adam. (f) Exercise budget: 15 exercises (8 ★, 6 ★★, 1 ★★★) total 130 minutes, the top of the allowed range; the coding practice is concentrated in the 185 minutes of labs. A ★ exercise is conceptual, with no arithmetic beyond quoting the text, which is why e3, e6, e12 and e13 are reasoning questions (regrading them to ★★ would break the 130-minute cap). No exercise reuses a worked example's numbers or is answered by an inline check: e1 (b) asks about a single ReLU, because s1's first check and the playground numbers answer 'no activation'; e7 uses ½(θ₁² + 64θ₂²); e10 uses p = 0.4 (s11's check uses 0.2); e11 uses the logits (800, 803, 799) and float64's overflow (s12 uses (1000, 999, 998) and float16's); e14 (b) is a late spike, because s14's first check covers an initial loss of 47; and s8's third check asks about rotation, so that it does not answer e9. SERIES CONVENTIONS. FLOPs: Module 06 owns the convention (in FLOP counts N is the weights used in matrix products, attention adds a context-dependent term, training costs three forward passes, memory counts every parameter); s2 states it once and links Module 06, Section 11, and s3 keeps only the argument that backward ≤ 2 × forward, linking Module 06 for the training count. No 6N formula appears in this module, and the attention formula appears only in Module 06. This module owns the softmax Jacobian (s3), the layer-norm and RMSNorm worked examples (s10) and the activation table (s5); Module 06 recalls them with a link back. Cross-references to other modules are always 'Module NN' (the source's 'Tutorial NN' never reaches the page). In the Chinese edition RMSNorm is 均方根归一化（RMSNorm）at first use, as in Module 06. TOPIC OWNERSHIP: do not re-derive Module 01's losses from maximum likelihood, the binary logistic gradient, ridge regression or the bias–variance decomposition; recall them in one sentence each and link. Module 01's outline also derives three things this module uses, so they are recalled rather than re-derived: the softmax-regression gradient p̂ − y case by case (s3 re-derives it only through the softmax Jacobian, as matrix-calculus practice), the SGD noise floor V ≈ ηs²/(2Bλ) (s9 measures it on a network), and early stopping as approximate ridge through filter factors (s11 adds the network procedure). Module 01 defers temperature scaling for networks to this module; s11 covers it with Lab 4's numbers. Module 01's gradient check uses the vector relative error ‖g_num − g‖/‖g_num + g‖; Lab 1 and s14 use the per-entry |a − n|/max(10⁻⁸, |a| + |n|), which localises a bug to a tensor — say once that both are relative errors. The Module 03 outline points to 'the training loop of Module 02, Section 10' (the source's numbering); in this module the loop is s13, and Lab 4 writes the model as an nn.Module subclass because Module 03 builds on that form.Module 03 owns ResNet, augmentation recipes and group norm in CNNs; Module 04 owns backpropagation through time, LSTM gates and their bias initialisation; Module 06 owns norm placement, SwiGLU and the residual stream; Module 08 owns mixed precision and loss scaling in depth, memory accounting, large-batch learning-rate scaling, warmup–stable–decay schedules and loss spikes at scale. Physics-informed networks (Module 05) are the pointer for forward-mode differentiation with respect to inputs. PUBLIC SITE: no mention of the private platform, its paths, plans or agents. The engineering flavour comes from the inputs-in-millimetres exercise (e15), the neo-Hookean extension of Lab 1, the noisy sensor-like regression of Lab 3, and the trajectory-sensitivity example of forward mode in s4. TRAPS: Nesterov's step-size limit on a quadratic is smaller than heavy ball's (and than GD's); do not call it 'more stable'. Adam and RMSProp are not rotation-invariant; GD and momentum are. The uncorrected-Adam step is too large only because β₂ is closer to 1 than β₁ (with β₂ = 0.95 it starts too small). PyTorch's BatchNorm momentum is the weight of the new value. CosineAnnealingLR's T_max counts scheduler.step() calls. torch.optim.Adam(decoupled_weight_decay=True) exists in the lab environment's PyTorch; write 'recent versions'. Date statements about current practice ('as of 2026'): SiLU/SwiGLU and RMSNorm in most open LLMs, dropout often off in LLM pretraining, warmup–stable–decay schedules. Checks are inline, with answers in a collapsed block.
